Adams County offices

Quincy anchors Adams County, the westernmost county in Illinois, which touches Missouri along its western edge. A property sale touches four offices: the collector, the Supervisor of Assessments, a township assessor and the Board of Review.

The collector, who is also the county treasurer, sends bills and takes payments at 507 Vermont St, Suite G12, Quincy (217-277-2245). The Supervisor of Assessments runs exemptions and equalization. The Board of Review hears assessment complaints in the Adams County Courthouse. The county has 23 townships, so a house outside Quincy is usually valued by a township assessor and not by a city office.

About the local market: population is 64,267 for 2025, down from 65,737 in 2020. Owners live in 72.1% of households, the middle owned home is worth $162,600, and renters typically pay $828.

How the tax cycle works for a seller

Bills trail the assessment by a year. An assessment reflects the home's value and exemptions on January 1, and the tax on it is paid the following year. A seller who closes mid-year therefore still owes for a stretch the county has not yet billed.

After a deed is recorded, the owner of record answers for later bills. Mailing happens in late spring. The first installment falls around June 1, or 30 days after mailing if that is later, and the second around September 1. A buyer may pay both halves at once or in two equal payments.

Typical Adams County collection calendar
StepUsual timing
Real estate bills mailedLate spring
First installment dueAround June 1, or 30 days after mailing if later
Second installment dueAround September 1
$10 mail and publication fee addedAround October 1
Last day to pay before the saleLate October
Annual tax saleLate October

Several dates are tentative each year, so ask the collector for the calendar covering the tax year you are closing in.

Late payments and the tax sale

For tax paid after September 30, the collector accepts a cashier's check, money order, cash or a card. Personal, business and e-checks are turned away. State law sets late interest at 1 1/2% per month or fraction of a month, and mail postmarked by the due date counts as on time (35 ILCS 200/21-15).

After the October fee the county publishes its list of delinquent parcels, and one last day remains for card payments ahead of the sale. Clear any unpaid tax before then, since a parcel sold at tax sale clouds the title.

  • Ask the collector at 217-277-2245 whether an installment is open before you list.
  • A title agent's tax search puts any payoff on the settlement statement.
  • Hold on to the postmarked envelope or bank confirmation when you pay near a deadline.

Assessment and how to appeal

A home outside Cook County is assessed at 33 1/3 percent of market value. To check your own number, divide the assessed value by what you think the home would sell for, then compare that ratio with similar homes nearby.

Put your complaint to the Board of Review in writing. In a county with fewer than 150,000 residents the filing date is August 10, though a missed publishing date can push it back. Sessions are usually Monday through Thursday, 8:30 to 11:30 a.m., from July 10 to October 7. The Board reads your complaint and mails a tentative decision. After that you can request a hearing, with or without an attorney.

A tax bill is outside the Board's reach. What it adjusts is the assessment behind the bill, and once it adjourns it prints the list of changes in a county newspaper. Still unhappy? Appeal in writing to the State Property Tax Appeal Board.

  • Strong grounds: a value estimate above what the home would sell for, wrong lot or building measurements, or an assessment above those of similar neighbors.
  • Helpful evidence: your deed or transfer declaration, a current appraisal, nearby comparable sales with photos, and the property record card.
  • A complaint filed late cannot fix a bill that has already gone out.

Homeowner exemptions

Each amount below comes off equalized assessed value and not the bill itself. The Supervisor of Assessments can tell you which ones fit your situation.

  • General homestead: the growth in equalized value since 1977, to a ceiling of $6,000, where the owner lives in the house.
  • Senior citizens: $5,000 off equalized value, available at 65.
  • Senior assessment freeze: household income capped at $75,000, renewed each year.
  • Homestead improvement: value from new construction, at most $75,000 a year, running four years after the work is finished and occupied.
  • Returning service members: $5,000 for two consecutive years.
  • Disabled persons: $2,000, applied for every year.
  • Disabled service members, standard exemption: $2,500 for a rating from 30% up to 50%, $5,000 from 50% up to 70%, and total relief from 70%.

Nearly all require you to live in the house. A buyer therefore files a fresh application once they hold title.

Senior tax deferral

Owners who qualify may put off as much as $7,500 of tax a year under the state's Senior Citizens Real Estate Tax Deferral Program. The deferral accrues simple interest at 3 percent from tax year 2023 on, and the county places a lien on the house. To apply you must be 65 by June 1, earn $65,000 or less as a household, and have lived three years in the home or a similar qualifying one.

A sale or transfer cannot legally close and record until the deferred amounts are paid, and the balance comes due 90 days after a sale. Filing is in person at the treasurer's office from January 1 through March 1. If you hold a deferral, get a payoff figure from the treasurer early and have it settled from your proceeds.

Ways to pay

The collector's office is inside the North 5th Street entrance of the courthouse, staffed on weekdays from half past eight until half past four.

  • Online by e-check or card: $1.50 per e-check and 2.25% of the payment for cards ($2.00 minimum).
  • A drop box outside the North 5th Street entrance, open around the clock (no cash).
  • Mail to Adams County Collector, 507 Vermont St STE G12, Quincy, IL 62301-2998, where the postmark date counts.
  • Participating banks, for real estate tax only and never after the due date.
  • Bank bill pay, using the full parcel number without dashes as the account.

Tax records and duplicate bills are online at no charge through the county's tax lookup.

Taxes and splits at closing

The closing statement may include a credit from the seller for estimated unbilled and unpaid tax. The exact figure is unknown until bills are created. In most cases the new owner receives the next bill and pays the seller's share. Give the buyer or title company a mailing address, since the county uses one address for bills, assessment notices and legal notices.

The office pauses deed and address updates for one to two weeks in mid-April while bills are produced. Splits and combined parcels recorded after August 10 do not take effect until January of the next tax year, and the original owner still gets the original bill. Decide in the contract who pays it.

Frequently asked questions

When are Adams County property tax installments due?

Around June 1 (or 30 days after mailing if later) and around September 1. The date printed on your bill is the one that counts.

What if my Quincy-area tax bill never arrives?

Phone the collector at 217-277-2245. Tax records and duplicate bills are online at no charge.

Can I appeal my Adams County assessment after August 10?

Not normally. For counties under 150,000 residents that is the Board of Review filing date, though it can be extended when publishing dates were missed. Ask the Supervisor of Assessments which date applies to your township.

Will the senior deferral stop me from selling a house in Adams County?

It will not stop a sale, but it must be paid first. No transfer may be closed and recorded until deferred taxes and interest are paid, so request a payoff early.

Does the Board of Review lower my tax bill directly?

No. It changes the assessment, and the bill is then built from the new value. The Board has no authority to change a tax bill itself.

Boone County at a glance

Boone County sits in far northern Illinois along the Wisconsin line, in the Rockford metro area. Belvidere serves as seat and biggest city. Nine townships make up the county: Belvidere, Bonus, Boone, Caledonia, Flora, Leroy, Manchester, Poplar Grove and Spring.

Population is estimated at 53,568 for 2025, up two tenths of a percent from 2020. Ownership is common: 81.8% of households own, and the middle owned home is worth $216,900. Median rent is $1,041 a month.

Belvidere 100, Harvard 50, Hiawatha 426, North Boone 200 and Rockford 205 are the school districts that touch the county, and the one serving your street appears on your bill. Besides Belvidere, the incorporated places are Poplar Grove, Cherry Valley, Capron, Caledonia and Timberlane, plus the Candlewick Lake community. The southern townships lie on the broad floodplains of the Kishwaukee River and its tributaries, so owners there should ask an insurer about flood risk.

Offices that send and collect the bill

Work is split three ways. For bills and payments, the Treasurer is at the Boone County Administration Campus, 1212 Logan Avenue, Suite 104, Belvidere (815-544-2666). For exemption and assessment questions, call the Assessment Office, also called the Supervisor of Assessments, at 815-544-2958. The County Clerk lists real property and takes redemption after a tax sale.

A tax year moves through six steps in order. First the Clerk lists the property. Then the township assessor values it as of January 1, and the county office equalizes the townships to one-third of market value. After that the Board of Review hears complaints, the Clerk figures rates, and the Treasurer bills and collects. Where you are in that order tells you which window is still open.

Due dates and how to pay

Expect your bill in late April. Half is due June 1 and half September 1, or you can pay it all by June 1. Illinois law does not allow partial payments.

  • At nearly any bank in the county, bringing the whole bill if you want it stamped as proof.
  • By mail: write the check to the Boone County Treasurer and make sure the postmark is on or before the due date.
  • Using your bank's bill-pay, with the property number as the vendor account number.
  • Online with a card or e-check, which adds a convenience fee of up to 2.5%.
  • In person on Logan Avenue with cash, a check or a money order, weekdays from 8:30 to 5:00.

Cards cannot be used at the counter or by phone. Does a mortgage escrow account pay your tax? Look up the status on the treasurer's website a little before the deadline, and phone the lender if it still shows open.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Boone County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to appeal your assessment

Your written complaint goes to the Boone County Board of Review. It is due 30 days after the changes are published, or on September 10 when that is later. Forms and Board staff come from the Assessment Office.

To contest value, state what you think the property was worth on January 1 of the assessment year and back it up. Evidence can be a closing statement from a recent purchase, three or more comparable sales within a year of the assessment date, a recent appraisal, or income and expense statements for an investment property. If you claim unequal treatment, list the address, parcel number and assessed value of at least three comparison properties.

A tentative notice arrives by mail. To dispute it, phone the Assessment Office inside the time shown on the notice and book a hearing. Once the final notice comes, you have 30 days to take the case to the Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board in Springfield, and Circuit Court review follows if needed. Put the 30-day window on your calendar when the list is printed in the newspaper.

Exemptions and limits

The Assessment Office administers the homestead exemptions and the preferential assessments:

  • General homestead: the rise in equalized value since 1977 comes off, up to $6,000, for an owner-occupied home.
  • Senior citizens: $5,000 off for owners 65 and older. The first application, form PTAX-324, goes to the county assessment officer.
  • Senior assessment freeze: household income below $75,000 for 2025, with form PTAX-340 filed each year.
  • Homestead improvement: value added by new work, to a yearly maximum of $75,000, lasting four years.
  • Disabled persons: $2,000 off the primary residence.
  • Service-connected disability: $2,500 at a 30% to 49% rating, $5,000 at 50% to 69%, and the first $250,000 of value at 70% or more.

Under the Property Tax Extension Limitation Law, a taxing district's yearly increase stays at the lesser of 5 percent or inflation, with new construction added. No single bill is capped by it, because assessments and exemptions can still move one owner's total.

What happens if a bill goes unpaid

Timing below counts from the second installment date. Figures are approximate, since state statute controls them.

Unpaid-tax timeline in Boone County
WhenWhat happens
One day after the deadlineA 1.5% penalty attaches, then 1.5% more each month
About two weeks afterCertified delinquency notice and a $10.00 fee
About one month afterList of delinquent parcels printed in a local newspaper
About two months afterTax sale; investors pay the tax plus about $44.00 in fees
Within 4 1/2 months of sale"Take notice" mailed by the County Clerk
About 2 1/2 years after saleRedemption ends and the buyer may petition for a tax deed

The sale sets the redemption rate, which can climb to 18% per six months. Afterward you redeem through the County Clerk with cash, a cashier's check or a money order. No installment plan exists. Title does not change hands at the sale itself.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Boone County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Taxes when the house sells

At closing the seller normally credits the buyer for tax that has accrued, and the buyer takes on the next bill. A bill left unpaid is a lien on the parcel, so buyers should confirm that earlier tax was settled.

Before you list, gather your latest bill, any exemption forms you filed and a note on who pays the tax if a lender escrows it. Those papers answer most of what a buyer asks.

Billing runs in arrears, so a house that sells in the fall still has a bill coming. Have the credit put in writing, read every line of the settlement statement, and ask for a payment-status check on the parcel before you sign. If you are the seller, a quick call to the Treasurer before closing shows whether either installment is still open and avoids a late surprise.

Frequently asked questions

How long do Belvidere-area owners have to contest a value?

You have 30 days from publication of the changes, or until September 10 if that is later. A further 30 days follows the Board's final ruling for a state appeal.

Can the tax be split into two payments in Boone County?

Yes: June 1 and September 1 are the two installment dates. Each installment must be paid in full, as partial payments are not allowed.

Is there a surcharge for paying Boone County tax by card?

Yes, online. Card or e-check payments add a fee of up to 2.5%, shown at checkout, and the office cannot take cards in person or by phone.

What role does the County Clerk play after a Boone County tax sale?

The Clerk collects redemption money in certified funds and mails the tax buyer's take-notice letter within about 4 1/2 months of the sale. Payment plans are not accepted.

How do I reach the Boone County Assessment Office?

Call 815-544-2958 for questions about assessments, exemptions and address changes. The Treasurer, which handles bills and payments, is at 1212 Logan Avenue, Suite 104, Belvidere, at 815-544-2666.

Bureau County at a glance

Bureau County is a mostly rural county in north-central Illinois. Princeton is the biggest city and holds the courthouse. The county estimate for 2025 is 32,510 residents, and the county has 15,663 housing units with a 76.1% ownership rate. The median owned home is worth $126,900, so most sales here sit well below suburban Chicago prices. A buyer's inspector will likely look hard at the basement and roof, so fix obvious problems before you set a price.

Who handles property tax

Two offices of the county sit in the courthouse at 700 South Main Street in Princeton, open weekdays from eight to four. The treasurer, who doubles as county collector, prepares and collects the bills. The Supervisor of Assessments supports the township assessors, processes exemptions, and acts as clerk to the Board of Review.

Bureau County tax offices
OfficeWherePhoneHandles
Treasurer and CollectorRoom 103815-872-3241Bills, payments, tax sale
Supervisor of AssessmentsSuite 12815-875-6478Exemptions, equalization, appeals clerk

Each township has an elected assessor who finds and values property first, before the county reviews anything. If a bill arrives for a house you no longer own, tell the treasurer so it can be sent back promptly.

How and when to pay

Bureau County mails a single bill that you can pay in two installments, and it will not take a partial payment on either one. The state statute counts an installment as late after the later of June 1 or the day following the date shown on the bill (35 ILCS 200/21-15), so the coupon on your own bill is the date that counts. A bill that never shows up, or shows up late, does not wipe out the tax or the late charge.

  • In the office, pay by check or cash. Make checks payable to "Bureau County Collector."
  • By mail, send payment to Bureau County Collector, 700 S. Main St., Room 103, Princeton, IL 61356. A postmark on the due date is acceptable.
  • Online, pay by debit card, credit card or e-check through Illinois ePAY. This works only through the second installment due date.
  • If a mortgage company pays your bill, check with that company yourself that the payment went out.

Your canceled check works as the receipt. If you want a separate one, include a stamped, self-addressed envelope with your payment.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Bureau County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What a late payment costs

Three charges can stack up. Past the due date, interest accrues at 1.5% per installment per month, and the coupons print the late-payment schedule. A payment sent without the late fees comes back to you. A further $10.00 is added to any tax still unpaid after the second installment date, which covers publication and the certified delinquent notice.

After those notices are mailed, the collector takes only certified funds: a cashier's check, money order or cash. Personal and business checks are refused. At the end of each tax year the collector holds a sale of the tax on every parcel still unpaid.

Selling with taxes owed

If you have fallen behind, clear the balance before you list. An open delinquency shows up in the title search and can stall a closing. Call the treasurer at 815-872-3241 for the payoff on each installment, and ask for certified-funds instructions if delinquent notices have already been mailed.

A cash buyer can close faster than a buyer who needs a lender, which helps when you want the back taxes settled out of the sale proceeds on a short timeline. The title company will deduct what is owed at closing, so having the figure early avoids surprises on the settlement statement.

A practical order of steps: get the payoff from the treasurer, confirm which installments are open, pay certified funds if notices have gone out, and ask for a written receipt to hand the title company.

How an assessment appeal works

The standard for nonfarm property in Illinois is 33 1/3% of fair market value, and Bureau County's Board of Review rules apply it too. If you disagree with your value, file an appeal form with the Board's clerk, the Supervisor of Assessments, by the thirtieth day after your township's assessment list is published. Filing costs nothing. You need a separate form for each parcel unless the parcels are contiguous and similarly classified.

Complaints must be about market value or equity. A tax bill that simply feels too big is not a valid complaint. For a home, the Board looks for:

  • Proof of a recent sale or purchase of the property.
  • A recent appraisal from an Illinois certified appraiser, delivered within 30 calendar days after the filing deadline and prepared to professional standards.
  • At least three recent sales of comparable properties, or assessed values of comparables if equity is the issue.
  • Dated photographs if you claim a condition problem.

The Board sends a tentative notice, and an owner who is unhappy with it has ten days to schedule a hearing. Each hearing gets a 15-minute slot in the Supervisor of Assessments' office. Speak for yourself or send an Illinois attorney, but do not skip it, because a missed hearing can end in dismissal. An incomplete form is returned once, with ten more calendar days to fix it.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Bureau County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Exemptions before you list

Homestead exemptions are applied under state statute and Department of Revenue guidelines. Any application is due by December 31. The Supervisor of Assessments processes exemption, preferential assessment and abatement applications and applies them to eligible parcels.

Exemptions depend on who owns and lives in the home, so a buyer should expect to apply in their own name. As a seller, ask the Supervisor of Assessments which exemptions sit on your parcel and bring that list to the closing so credits are figured on real numbers. The county website carries the Board's rules and the appeal form, plus GIS imagery that shows parcel boundaries and aerial photos.

Property tax at closing

Because Illinois bills a year in arrears, the first bill after a sale usually covers time the seller owned the house. Many contracts deal with that through a seller credit at closing for tax not yet billed, and yours can spell it out. For the payment status of the parcel, call the treasurer's office at 815-872-3241.

  • Confirm whether both installments of the prior bill are paid.
  • Agree in the contract how the next bill will be split.
  • Give the county the buyer's mailing address so assessment notices and bills reach the right person.
  • Keep copies of the deed and transfer paperwork. The Board of Review accepts a recent purchase as evidence of value.
  • Bring a photo ID and the parcel number if you visit the treasurer's counter for a payoff figure.

Frequently asked questions

How many installments does Bureau County property tax have?

Two. One bill arrives and is payable in two installments, and the county refuses partial payments. The coupon on your bill shows each date.

Is there a fee to appeal a Bureau County assessment?

No. Filing an appeal with the Board of Review costs nothing. The deadline is the thirtieth day after your township's assessment list is published.

Can I pay Bureau County tax with a credit card?

Yes, online through Illinois ePAY by debit card, credit card or e-check, until the second installment due date. The treasurer's counter takes only checks and cash.

What happens to Bureau County tax I do not pay?

Interest builds at 1.5% per installment per month, $10.00 is added after the second installment date, and the collector holds a tax sale on unpaid parcels at year end. After notices go out, only certified funds are taken.

Where do I file a homestead exemption in Bureau County?

With the Supervisor of Assessments, 700 South Main Street, Suite 12, Princeton, phone 815-875-6478. December 31 is the deadline to apply.

Champaign County market context

Champaign County covers about 998 square miles of flat farmland and two linked cities, Champaign and Urbana, which nearly wrap around the University of Illinois campus. Urbana is the seat of government. Mid-2025 population is estimated at 209,972, with owners living in 54.0% of homes and a median owned-home value of $211,500. Those numbers describe the whole county, so a farmhouse east of I-57 and a campus-area duplex can look nothing alike on a tax bill. Price from nearby sales, and treat the countywide median as background only.

Who runs property tax in Champaign County

Four county offices split the job. Think of it as value, disputes, money and redemption: one office sets the number, one hears complaints, one sends the bill, and one deals with sold taxes.

  • Supervisor of Assessments: receives the work of the township assessors, mails change notices and processes homestead exemptions. The assessment office number is 217-384-3760.
  • Board of Review: a panel of three, appointed by the County Board once they pass a state exam. They hear complaints, equalize values between townships and add omitted property to the rolls.
  • Treasurer and Collector: sends out about 77,000 real estate bills a year and splits the money among 125 taxing districts. The office number is 217-384-3743.
  • County Clerk: takes redemptions once a tax sale has happened and works out the rates once every taxing body files its levy.

You will find the Treasurer inside the Scott M. Bennett Administrative Center, 102 E. Main Street, Urbana. About 3,400 mobile homes get separate bills, due sixty days after mailing.

How assessment and billing work

Each township assessor values property using a January 1 snapshot, then hands the results to the Supervisor of Assessments by June 15. The target is one-third of market value. When a township's level drifts away from that share, the Supervisor can apply a township multiplier, and those multipliers are published in newspapers and on the county website.

State revenue officials audit the county's assessment work every cycle. If it finds the work properly done, it issues a multiplier of 1.

Schools claim the biggest share. Each taxing body votes a levy by December 31 and sends it to the County Clerk, and state law caps most increases at growth in assessed value and the consumer price index. Mailing finishes by May 1. You owe the tax even if no bill reaches you, so call the Treasurer for another copy.

Payment dates and methods

Expect the bill in early May, with installments typically due in June and September. A postmark on the due date is good enough. Your coupon lists this year's exact dates.

State law adds interest of 1.5% for each month or partial month a payment is late, and each coupon prints a schedule. A payment returned for any reason is void, with a $30 charge plus statutory interest. Personal and business checks work through September 30. After that the counter wants cash, money orders, cashier's checks or certified checks.

  • Use a participating local bank from the list on the county website.
  • Mail the coupon and a check made out to Champaign County Collector to P.O. Box 4306, Springfield, IL 62708-4306.
  • Call 217-834-8713 or go online and use a card or eCheck with the property's PIN. A vendor fee applies.
  • Walk in to 102 E. Main Street, Urbana, weekdays 8 to 4:30, or use the 24-hour drop box in the parking lot.

How to challenge your valuation

Your window to complain to the Board of Review runs July 1 through September 10, and hearings happen inside it. Once it closes, members research values and put decisions in writing. The office keeps 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. hours Monday through Thursday, or sees people by appointment.

If you carry the dispute to the state Property Tax Appeal Board, the board speaks for the county there. Back up your number with paper: the closing statement from your purchase and nearby sales of similar homes.

Exemptions that lower the bill

An exemption comes off the equalized assessed value before the rate is applied. The bill drops, and nobody has decided your house is worth less.

Champaign County homeowner exemptions
ExemptionReductionWho qualifies
General homestead (Section 15-175)$6,000Owner's primary residence on January 1 of the assessment year
Senior citizens (Section 15-177)$5,000Owners who turn 65 by the end of the assessment year
Senior assessment freeze (Section 15-172)Holds value at a base yearHousehold income up to $75,000, renewed yearly with proof of income
Persons with disabilities (Section 15-168)$2,000Owners with a qualifying disability
Service-connected disability (Section 15-169)Scaled to the disability rating, up to the full assessed value at 70% or higherOwners with a qualifying service-connected disability

Forms by fax or email are not accepted, so call and ask for a mailed copy. If the house sells, ask whether your exemption ends and what the buyer needs to file.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Champaign County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What follows a missed payment

The house stays yours; the debt is what changes hands. The Collector sends a certified delinquent notice in October and prints the owner's name and amount in the newspaper. Whatever is unpaid after 4:30 p.m. on October 29 goes into the October 30 sale, where an investor pays the tax and gets a claim on the property.

Afterward you owe the sold amount plus interest at the sale-day rate. Roughly two weeks on, the County Clerk (217-384-3722) can give you the redemption figure, and the Clerk's Take Notice follows within four months. You pay the Clerk, who reimburses the investor. The usual period is 3 years from the sale date, with exceptions in 35 ILCS 200/21-350. If nobody redeems, the investor may petition the circuit court for a deed.

Checking taxes before closing

Read the closing statement closely. The Treasurer points both sides to the closing papers, the title company or the attorney for any tax owed. Depending on the closing date and when the deed is recorded, the next bill may still go to the previous owner, who has to pass it along.

No bill in hand? Request a duplicate by PIN and check whether either installment is open. When taxes are behind, find out what clearing them costs before closing, because unpaid taxes head toward the October sale. Anything open for the current year gets settled through the title company or attorney.

Have four items ready when you call: the property PIN, the closing date, the expected recording date and the buyer's mailing address. That lets the office say what is paid, what is open and where the next bill goes.

Frequently asked questions

Which office mails Champaign County tax bills?

The County Treasurer, who also acts as Collector, normally mails them in early May. You owe the tax even if a bill goes missing, and 217-384-3743 gets you a duplicate.

What is the Champaign County appeal window?

File with the Board of Review between July 1 and September 10. After that date members research values and issue written decisions.

Are personal checks taken at the counter after September 30?

No. Personal and business checks stop on September 30. From October 1 the counter takes cash, money orders, cashier's checks and certified checks only.

Does a tax sale mean I lose my house?

Not right away. Only the unpaid tax is sold, and you can redeem it through the County Clerk with interest. A court deed comes into play only if the redemption period runs out.

How much is the general homestead exemption in Champaign County?

It is a $6,000 cut in equalized assessed value for an owner-occupied primary residence. Call 217-384-3760 to get the application mailed.

Coles County, IL Property Tax Guide: Offices, Appeals and Selling With Tax Due

Cash Home Buyers in Illinois
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Coles County, IL Property Tax Guide sale

Selling in Coles County? Get a Cash Offer

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Coles County?

Which offices handle property tax

Two courthouse offices split the work. The Supervisor of Assessments and the Board of Review set and review values, and the Collector/Treasurer bills and takes payment. Both are in the Coles County Courthouse at 651 Jackson Ave in Charleston, with the Board of Review in Room 133 and the treasurer in Room 124.

Complaint forms go to the Supervisor of Assessments office, which is open from 8:30 in the morning until 4:30 in the afternoon on weekdays. The treasurer keeps the same hours and can be reached at (217) 348-0513.

  • Value, exemptions and appeals: Supervisor of Assessments and the three member Board of Review.
  • Bills, payments and the delinquent list: Coles County Collector/Treasurer.
  • Online look-up: the county's property tax inquiry portal shows assessment and tax data by parcel.

Coles County housing at a glance

Coles County is a prairie county of about 508 square miles in east central Illinois. Charleston is the seat and the home of Eastern Illinois University, and Mattoon is the other large city. The population is estimated at 46,607 for July 2025, down from 53,873 in 2010.

There are 22,693 housing units, and 60.4% of homes are owner occupied. The median owner occupied home is worth $127,400, median gross rent is $780, and monthly owner costs run $1,220 with a mortgage and $546 without one.

Tax dates in the Coles County cycle

Bills go out in the spring, with the first installment due around July 1 and the second around September 1. Late payments carry a 1.5% penalty unless the envelope is postmarked by the due date. Each year the treasurer posts exact dates on the Key Dates page, so use that page for the current cycle.

Typical Coles County tax calendar
EventTiming
Tax bills mailedMid-May
First installment dueJuly 1
Penalty on first installmentThe day after it is due
Second installment dueSeptember 1
Penalty increases on both installmentsEarly September and early October
Delinquent list published, last day to register for the saleEarly October
Tax sale, 11:30 a.m.Late October

The county splits each year's tax into two equal installments. Take a mailed payment inside the post office to be hand stamped, because a drop in a street box does not guarantee the right postmark.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Coles County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to pay a Coles County tax bill

Bring the original bill to the treasurer's office, which takes cash, checks and most credit cards. A payment drop box sits at the south entrance of the courthouse, and a second one is at Mattoon City Hall. Mail goes to the Coles County Collector, 651 Jackson Ave., Room 124, Charleston, IL 61920.

  • Banks: First Mid-Illinois Bank & Trust, Prospect Bank in Ashmore, First Farmers Bank & Trust in Oakland, Washington Savings Bank in Mattoon and several others are authorized pay points.
  • By card: phone 1-217-292-6625 or use the county tax portal at colescountyilretax.us. The card company charges a convenience fee, and an online check costs $1.00.
  • Prepayment: the treasurer accepts prepayments of any amount starting January 1, though it advises against paying more than last year's tax.

The last day for personal checks and card or e-check payments falls a couple of weeks before the sale, so pay early if you are close to the delinquent list.

Contesting an assessment

You appeal the assessed value, never the tax bill, and you start with the Board of Review. The board opens its session on the first Monday in June. The 2026 filing deadline is December 14, 2026, and the complaint forms say the deadline is 30 days after the Supervisor of Assessments publishes the assessments.

An early call to the assessor can sometimes fix a clerical error without a hearing. A written complaint to the Board of Review is required before any later appeal to the state Property Tax Appeal Board, and taxes stay payable while that appeal is pending. The state board's number is 217-782-6076.

  • A recent purchase on the open market or a professional appraisal supports a claim that the value is too high.
  • A wrong lot or building measurement is another ground.
  • Comparable homes, property record cards, photographs and a transfer declaration make up the evidence package.

Once the tax bill arrives it is too late to contest that year's assessment, so a seller with a recent price drop should act before the deadline.

When taxes go unpaid

Unpaid parcels appear on a delinquent list published in a newspaper, then go to the annual tax sale. Buyers register by the date on the key dates list, file a letter of intent and pay a $250 registration fee that is applied to purchases. New buyers also need a letter of credit from their bank.

A sale does not move the deed. It places the unpaid tax in a buyer's hands, and the owner can pay it back during a redemption period. Ask the treasurer or clerk for the redemption deadline and payoff figure on any sold parcel before you list or sign a contract.

Mobile homes follow a separate track. Bills are mailed between March and May for the calendar year and are due 60 days after mailing. Interest runs $25 per month, capped at $100. A buyer needs a Mobile Home Certification filed with the Secretary of State to get clear title, and the treasurer can issue it once taxes are paid.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Coles County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling checklist

Start with the parcel's tax history and ask your title company how both installments will be handled at closing. Then look at deadlines and paperwork.

  • Pull the parcel record on the county portal and confirm the bill name and mailing address.
  • Ask the treasurer whether any installment shows penalty and what the payoff is on a given day.
  • Check whether an appeal is open, since the 2026 filing window runs to December 14.
  • Gather repair estimates and any appraisal, since both support an appeal and a price discussion.

A home needing repairs can go to a cash buyer as is, and a tax payoff is taken from the sale proceeds.

What to bring when you visit the courthouse: your parcel number, the original bill if you still have it, and a photo ID. The treasurer in Room 124 can give you the payoff on a given day, and the Supervisor of Assessments can tell you which exemptions sit on the parcel. Do both before the title company orders its payoff, so the figures match. If the buyer is financing, the lender will usually want proof that both installments for the year are paid or escrowed.

Frequently asked questions

When is the Coles County property tax deadline?

The first installment is due around July 1 and the second around September 1. A 1.5% penalty applies to payments postmarked after the due date.

Where do I file a Coles County assessment complaint?

With the Supervisor of Assessments office in the courthouse at 651 Jackson Ave, Charleston, during weekday office hours. The Board of Review meets in Room 133. The 2026 filing deadline is December 14, 2026.

Can I pay Coles County taxes by card?

Yes. The treasurer accepts most credit and debit cards in the office, by phone and online. The card company charges a convenience fee, and an online check costs $1.00.

What is the Coles County tax sale?

It is the yearly auction of unpaid real estate tax, held in late October at 11:30 a.m. Buyers pay a $250 registration fee, and owners keep a redemption period to pay the amount back.

Does an appeal lower my Coles County tax bill right away?

No. An appeal challenges the assessed value, and any change flows into a later bill. You must keep paying while a state Property Tax Appeal Board case is pending.

Cook County at a glance

Cook County is the most populous county in Illinois and the second most populous in the United States, with more than 40 percent of the state's residents. It covers 945 square miles of land, includes the city of Chicago, and counts more than 800 local governmental units. Outside Chicago and Evanston the county is split into 29 townships, and Chicago keeps its old township lines for assessment purposes.

The 2025 population was 5,194,625, with 2,292,484 housing units. About 57.7% of homes are owner occupied, the median owned home is valued at $324,500, and median gross rent is $1,435. Those are countywide medians across Chicago and the suburbs, so look up the specific PIN for the bill on a particular house.

Who does what

Cook County bills property tax through its Treasurer at 118 N. Clark Street in Chicago and values property through the Assessor and the Board of Review.

Cook County offices that touch a home sale
OfficeWhat it does for a seller
TreasurerSends bills, takes payments, runs the annual tax sale and issues refunds
AssessorSets the estimated market value and takes first-level appeals
Board of ReviewHears a second round of appeals after the Assessor
County ClerkRecords deeds, which matters at closing

Installment due dates

Cook County's installment dates change from year to year. The Treasurer's Due Dates page lists each installment by tax year, and the second bill for a year can land in the next calendar year. In recent years the first installment has fallen between March 1 and April 1, and the second has moved between August 1 and December 15.

Ask the Treasurer for the current due date and the status of each PIN instead of assuming last year's schedule. The Treasurer's site offers a payment plan calculator, a payment status check, online payment from a bank account or card, mail and in-person payment, and payment at Chase Bank and at local community banks. It also has forms to update a name or mailing address and a page on monitoring your mortgage, both useful when a sale changes who receives the bill.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Cook County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Reassessment and appeals

The Assessor reassesses one part of the county each year on a three year cycle. In 2026 the south and west suburbs are reassessed, and every owner there receives a Reassessment Notice with the property's characteristics and new estimated fair market value. The north suburbs and the City of Chicago are reassessed only when something changes, such as a permit or division work.

An owner may appeal to the Assessor's Office and, separately, to the Board of Review. The Assessor's calendar lists a notice date and a last file date for each township, and the Board of Review appeal periods open after the roll is certified. Updated values appear online one business day after the mailing date, and by law the assessment roll must also be published in a print newspaper. Check your township on the calendar for the exact window.

If you own in the south and west suburbs, read the Reassessment Notice as soon as it arrives. It lists the characteristics the Assessor has on file for your property, and an error there, such as the wrong square footage, is the easiest thing to fix.

When you appeal, bring paper that supports your number: a recent purchase price, an appraisal and sales of similar homes. Because the Assessor and the Board of Review keep separate dates, a missed first window does not always close the second, but do not count on it.

How the tax sale works

The Treasurer holds an annual sale of delinquent taxes. The sale scheduled to begin December 15, 2026 covers delinquent tax year 2023 taxes and special assessments, and it runs from 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. on each sale day. Townships are grouped by day: December 15 starts with Barrington, Berwyn, Bloom, Bremen, Calumet, Cicero, Elk Grove, Evanston and the other alphabetically early townships through Orland, and later days continue through Hyde Park, Jefferson, Lake, Lake View and the rest. A re-offer day follows on December 21.

The sale is online at the county's tax sale site, and final bids can only be placed from computers in the Treasurer's sale room at 118 N. Clark Street, Room 112. Buyers register by December 4, 2026 and post collateral. The delinquency lists cost $250 for the general tax list and $250 for the special assessment list.

Parcels are offered as is, and the PIN alone, not the street address, identifies the delinquent taxes. A homeowner can search any PIN on the Treasurer's website to see whether taxes are delinquent. The site has a page titled "If Taxes Were Sold" for owners whose parcel was already sold.

Exemptions and relief programs

The Treasurer's menu links to several programs that matter when a house changes hands or an owner is on a fixed income.

  • Homeowner exemption and senior citizen homestead exemption.
  • Senior citizen assessment freeze and the Senior Citizen Real Estate Tax Deferral Program.
  • Persons with disability, home improvement and disabled veteran exemptions.
  • Property tax relief for military personnel and a first responder surviving spouse abatement.
  • Certificate of Error and refund forms, including an overpayment refund search.

Ask the Treasurer which exemptions appear on your PIN, and read each program page for its own rules.

What to do about taxes before selling

Gather the PIN, the last two bills and the township name, then compare them with the Assessor's calendar to see whether an appeal window is open. Check the delinquent search, and if your parcel appears on a tax sale list, contact the Treasurer before signing a contract.

  • Search the PIN for delinquent taxes on the Treasurer's website.
  • Confirm your township on the Assessor's calendar and read the last file date.
  • Ask your title company to include every unpaid installment in the payoff figures.
  • Record the deed with the County Clerk after closing.

At closing, the title company normally orders a payoff for every open installment and pays it from your proceeds. Cook County bills run in two parts and the second often arrives after a sale, so ask how the title company plans to credit the buyer for the time you owned the house. The new owner should send the Treasurer a mailing address update, using the Treasurer's name and address change forms, so the next bill reaches the right person.

Cash buyers can close around an unpaid installment, since the payoff comes out of the sale proceeds. You still need the figure in writing before you accept an offer.

Frequently asked questions

When is the Cook County second installment due?

The date changes every year, and the second bill for a tax year can land in the next calendar year. Recent second installments have fallen between August 1 and December 15, so check the Treasurer's Due Dates page.

Which parts of Cook County are reassessed in 2026?

The south and west suburbs. The north suburbs and Chicago are reassessed only when a change occurs, such as a permit. The Assessor mails each owner a Reassessment Notice.

Can I appeal to both the Assessor and the Board of Review?

Yes. Owners may appeal to the Assessor's Office and to the Board of Review, and each has its own dates. Check the township listing for both.

When is the next Cook County annual tax sale?

The sale for delinquent tax year 2023 taxes is scheduled to begin December 15, 2026 at 8:30 a.m. A re-offer day is listed for December 21. Search your PIN on the Treasurer's site to see whether it is eligible.

Where does Cook County send property tax payments?

Payments can be made online with a bank account or card, by mail or in person, at Chase Bank, or at local community banks. The Treasurer's office is at 118 N. Clark Street in Chicago.

DuPage County, IL Property Tax Guide: Offices, Appeals and Selling With Tax Due

Cash Home Buyers in Illinois
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • DuPage County, IL Property Tax Guide: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a DuPage County, IL Property Tax Guide sale
  • Turn the DuPage County, IL Property Tax Guide offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling in DuPage County? Get a Cash Offer

We buy DuPage County houses as-is and reply with a written cash offer.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in DuPage County?
We buy DuPage County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Which DuPage County offices deal with property tax

The work is split four ways. One office oversees the nine township assessors and posts assessment changes (the Supervisor of Assessments), another hears appeals (the Board of Review), a third sends bills and takes money (the Treasurer), and the County Clerk deals with redemption once taxes have been sold.

  • Supervisor of Assessments: 630-407-5858, for exemption and assessment questions.
  • Board of Review: 630-407-5888, for complaint hearings.
  • County Treasurer: bills, payment, the delinquent list and the annual sale.
  • County Clerk: 630-407-5500, for a redemption estimate on sold taxes, and 630-407-5540 to change a billing name or address.

Assessment questions start with the township assessor named on your tax bill. The nine townships are Wayne, Bloomingdale, Addison, Winfield, Milton, York, Naperville, Lisle and Downers Grove.

DuPage County housing at a glance

DuPage County sits directly west of Chicago. Wheaton is the county seat and Naperville is the largest city. The county covers about 327 square miles of land, and almost all of it is developed. The population was 934,298 in July 2025, with 370,517 housing units.

Owners occupy 73.1% of homes. The median owned home is valued at $391,400, median household income is $112,096 and median gross rent is $1,688.

When bills come due

You get a single bill a year with two payment coupons. It goes out starting in late April. The first coupon is due June 1 and the second September 1. State law charges 1.5% interest a month on a late installment, and the U.S. postmark settles whether a mailed payment was on time.

Late taxes follow a set path toward the sale. Pre-delinquent bills go out in late September, with a payment deadline in early October to stay off the newspaper list. The delinquent list is published in mid-October, and certified delinquent bills are mailed soon after. From November 2 only cash, a cashier's check or a money order is accepted, and an extra $10 covers the publication and certified mailing. This year the last day to pay is November 18 by 4:30 p.m., and the sale for unpaid 2025 taxes begins November 19.

The bill lists the parcel number (PIN), the township assessor, the tax code, the fair cash value and an equalized value of one third of fair cash value. Keep the PIN handy, since it identifies the property in every county office.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your DuPage County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Appeal deadlines by township

Every township sets its own cutoff, 30 days after that township's assessments are published. The Supervisor of Assessments posts the dates on its Assessment Status page. Townships open and close one after another through the fall. Winfield, parcel prefix 04, is the last of the nine, with a final complaint date of November 23, 2026.

Chatting with the township assessor does not pause the clock at the Board of Review. File inside the window even if the conversation is not finished, because a late filing is thrown out.

How a DuPage County assessment appeal works

Appeals must be filed electronically in the county's SmartFile system, and anything outside the 30 day window is rejected. Start by calling or visiting the township assessor to check your property record. If the value still looks too high, file.

Plan to submit three or more comparables. Recent sales are needed to argue market value, while similar homes with matching features are what a uniformity claim needs. Values are built on the prior three years of sales, so the 2025 value used 2022, 2023 and 2024.

  • A recent appraisal or a recent sale of your own house is the best evidence.
  • Written decisions are mailed after all county hearings finish, usually the following March.
  • A decision can be appealed to the Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board within 30 days of the notice.

Behind the scenes, township assessors finish their entries by November 15 of the assessment year, the Supervisor of Assessments applies a township equalization factor where needed, and the state can add its own factor before the Clerk computes rates.

Exemptions

Each exemption lowers taxable value. After closing, a new owner should ask the township assessor how to apply.

DuPage County exemptions
ExemptionAmountHow to get it
ResidentialUp to $8,000Home lived in on or before January 1 of the tax year; the township assessor initiates it
Senior citizens homesteadUp to $8,000Proof of age and ownership
Senior assessment freezeHolds assessed valueHousehold income limit of $65,000, with an application
Disabled persons$2,000 a year off assessed valueAnnual application
Homestead improvementUp to $25,000 of added assessmentApplies to improvements, for up to four years

Owners who qualify as disabled or returning service members can call the Supervisor of Assessments at 630-407-5858.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy DuPage County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

If DuPage County taxes are sold

At the Treasurer's sale, bidders compete on interest rate. The lowest rate wins, and that bidder pays the unpaid tax for the owner. The legal maximum bid is 9%, and the average winning bid was 2% per six month period in November 2025. A buyer pays the tax, interest and $124.00 in costs per parcel, then holds a certificate of purchase that acts as a lien.

You keep title while the redemption clock runs. The minimum is 2 1/2 years for residential property of one to six units and 2 years for other classes, which a buyer may extend to 3 years. After that the buyer can petition the circuit court for a tax deed.

If your taxes were sold, call the Clerk for an estimate of redemption and share it with your title company. The sale is not reported to credit agencies.

Selling with a DuPage County bill open

A bill mailed in spring covers the prior tax year, because Illinois bills in arrears. Before you list, confirm that both installments on the latest bill are paid, and have the title company explain how the buyer will be credited for your months of ownership. Have the PIN, the township assessor's name and your last bill ready.

If you are behind, pay before the delinquent list comes out, because a sold tax adds interest, costs and a redemption estimate to the closing. A cash buyer can often close around an open bill, but the payoff still comes out of your proceeds. After closing, the new owner can ask the County Clerk at 630-407-5540 to change the billing name or address, so the next bill is mailed to the right person and not forwarded through you.

A short list for the title company: the PIN, the township assessor's name, the latest bill, and any exemption shown on it.

Frequently asked questions

When is the second installment due in DuPage County?

September 1. The first installment is due June 1. Illinois law adds 1.5% interest per month to a late installment.

Can I still appeal if my township's window has closed?

No. The window ends 30 days after the township's assessments are published, and late appeals are rejected. Next year's schedule appears on the Supervisor of Assessments' Assessment Status page.

How do I file a DuPage County assessment appeal?

File it electronically through the county's SmartFile system, which the Board of Review requires. Attach at least three comparable properties. Hearing decisions are mailed the following March.

What is the redemption period after the DuPage County tax sale?

At least 2 1/2 years for a residential property of one to six units and 2 years for other property. A buyer can stretch the final date to 3 years. Call the County Clerk at 630-407-5500 for an estimate.

Who do I call about a DuPage County exemption?

Call the Supervisor of Assessments at 630-407-5858 or your township assessor. The residential and senior exemptions are each up to $8,000, and the senior freeze has a $65,000 income limit.

Who handles property tax in Effingham County

Responsibility is divided among four offices. Assessments are built and defended by the Supervisor of Assessments, disputes go to the Board of Review, and the Treasurer, acting as county collector, sends the bills and takes payment. Rates and post-sale redemption belong to the County Clerk.

  • Treasurer: 217-342-6844, County Office Building, 101 N. Fourth Street, Effingham, open weekdays from eight to four
  • Supervisor of Assessments: 217-342-6711, also the office to call when your mailing address for tax bills changes
  • Board of Review: meets on the fourth floor of the same building
  • County Clerk: 217-342-8433 for tax rates and levies, 217-342-6535 for redemption estimates

The county's online parcel search, reached through its property tax inquiry link, pulls up a bill by owner name or address. Have the ten-digit parcel number handy if you have it. It prints at the left side of the bill, under the owner's name.

Due dates and the billing cycle

Effingham County bills in two installments. For 2025 taxes payable in 2026, those were September 25 and November 6, and both are behind us. Dates are set each year when bills go out, so the stubs on your own bill are the final word.

Illinois collects a year behind, which the county calls a two-year cycle. Year one fixes each parcel's value as of January 1. Year two applies the rates, mails the bills and sends the proceeds to the taxing districts. The 2025 bills went out on August 21, 2026, and the Treasurer asks anyone who hasn't received one by September 11 to call. A missing bill is no excuse: the tax and any late penalty still apply.

The county collects for more than 90 taxing districts. It also bills drainage, mobile home and railroad taxes.

Ways to pay

You can pay by mail, in person, at a bank or online. Bring or send the original bill, or one printed from the county website. Other paperwork carries a $1 copy fee.

  • By mail, with the installment stub and a check, postmarked no later than the due date
  • At the Treasurer's counter
  • At most banks in the county, but only while the bill is not yet late, because banks can't take past-due payments
  • Online by credit card or e-check, which adds a convenience fee and can take up to seven days to post

With an escrow account, your lender may want a copy of the bill, so ask. Once you've sold, and the closing statement leaves the tax to the buyer, pass any bill that reaches you along to the new owner.

Late payment and the tax sale

Delinquent tax picks up a 1.5% penalty each month, and the amount rises every 30 days. After the due date, only the Treasurer's office can take payment, by mail or online. For the 2025 taxes payable in 2026, the county's remaining steps run like this:

Effingham County delinquent tax steps, 2025 taxes payable in 2026
StepDateWhat happens
Certified delinquent noticesNovember 30, 2026Mailed with a $10 per parcel fee; no personal or business checks afterward
Online payment cutoffDecember 27, 2026Last day to pay by card or e-check
Tax saleJanuary 7, 2027Held in the North room of the County Office Building

The sale is of the unpaid tax, not of the house, and a payer can still settle up to one business day before it. The county has elected under Public Act 104-0553 to acquire all delinquent taxes as trustee for the taxing districts. After a sale, ask the County Clerk for a redemption estimate.

How to appeal your assessment

Your written complaint is due at the Board of Review 30 calendar days after the newspaper prints your township's assessment changes. Publication dates differ by township, so find the paper that covers yours. The Supervisor of Assessments hands out parcel-specific appeal forms at 217-342-6711 or assessor@effinghamcountyil.gov.

The Board hears testimony on property claimed to be over-assessed or under-assessed and either confirms the value or corrects it. Hearings wrap up in early February. Still unhappy afterward? Your next stops are the Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board or circuit court.

Before you send anything in, get the Board's current rules and filing information. Keep a copy of every page you submit.

Exemptions and the payment plan

First-time exemption applications go to the Supervisor of Assessments' office, and renewal forms are mailed each February. The exemptions on the county's list are senior homestead and assessment freeze, annual lease agreement, home improvement, returning veteran (PTAX-341), disabled veteran (PTAX-342) and disabled person (PTAX-343). Dollar amounts come from state law and shift over time, so ask that office what applies now.

The Treasurer also helps senior citizens apply for the state real estate tax deferral and approves those who qualify.

An optional nine-month prepayment plan, called TREASURER 9, spreads next year's tax over monthly payments due on the 15th. It currently runs January through August, costs nothing and requires that you owe no delinquent taxes. Sign up by October 15. Payments follow the most recent tax amount for the parcel.

Effingham County housing at a glance

Effingham County is in south central Illinois, anchored by the city of Effingham, its seat and biggest town, with Interstate 70 running through. Population is 34,519 with 15,520 housing units. Owner-occupied homes carry a median value of $189,500, and homeowners live in 78.2% of the units. Median household income is $80,404 and median gross rent is $733.

Selling with taxes owed

How the tax is split is a negotiation between the two sides. The county tells anyone who bought in late 2025 or 2026 to check the closing papers or ask the closing agent whether tax is still owed, because the bill may have been addressed to the previous owner depending on recording dates.

If you're selling and the bill is unpaid, here is the order of work:

  • Pull the bill from the online parcel search or call the Treasurer.
  • Ask the collector's office for the exact balance, including penalty, so the title company can quote it.
  • If the parcel already went to a tax sale, ask the County Clerk for a redemption estimate.
  • Confirm the ten-digit parcel number on the contract matches the bill.
  • Pay the balance at closing from proceeds, or before the sale date if one is close.

A cash sale skips the lender's payoff process, but the tax still has to be settled with the collector before the title can clear.

Frequently asked questions

When is the second installment of Effingham County property tax due?

For 2025 taxes payable in 2026, the first installment was due September 25 and the second November 6. Bills go out in late summer and show exact dates on the stubs.

What does paying Effingham County taxes late cost?

Late tax costs 1.5% for each month, growing every 30 days. Once the due date passes, banks can't take the payment, so it goes to the Treasurer's office by mail, in person or online.

Does Effingham County sell my house if I don't pay property tax?

No. The tax sale is a sale of the unpaid tax, and the buyer charges interest on top. You can pay until one business day before the sale, or redeem afterward through the County Clerk.

Where does an Effingham County assessment appeal go?

To the Board of Review, within 30 calendar days after your township's assessment changes are published. Get the parcel-specific form from the Supervisor of Assessments at 217-342-6711.

Which Effingham County office explains my tax rate?

The County Clerk, at 217-342-8433, computes rates from each district's levy. The Supervisor of Assessments at 217-342-6711 covers assessed value and exemptions, and the Treasurer at 217-342-6844 handles bills and payments.

County offices and phone numbers

Franklin County handles property tax from the Government Annex Building at 901 Public Square in Benton, the county seat. A single number, 618-435-9800, reaches the Treasurer, the Supervisor of Assessments and the Board of Review. Offices keep weekday hours from eight in the morning to four in the afternoon.

  • Treasurer: collects the bill, takes mail at PO Box 967, Benton, IL 62812, and runs the delinquent tax sale
  • Supervisor of Assessments: the chief county assessment officer, who handles exemptions and mailing address changes
  • Board of Review: three county citizens appointed by the County Board, with the chief assessment officer as clerk
  • County Clerk: explains how to pay delinquent taxes after a sale

Township assessors set the starting values. The county has assessors for Goode/Barren, Benton, Browning, Cave/Eastern, Denning, Ewing/Northern, Frankfort, Six Mile and Tyrone, so phone the assessment office to find out who covers your parcel.

How your bill is figured

Two numbers drive the bill: the value your township assessor puts on the property, and the money your local taxing districts say they need for the coming year. The assessment office likens it to income tax, a rate applied to a base.

Roughly 60% of what's collected goes to education. The rest is divided among the county, cities, park districts, library districts, fire districts, townships and other special districts, more than fifty local governments in all. The school district where the property sits takes the biggest share.

Assessments can drop while rates climb, since a rate depends on the district's total levy and its total equalized assessed value. The Treasurer's page posts a rate report for 2025 taxes payable in 2026, and your own bill shows the rate for each of your taxing districts.

A parcel inside a tax increment finance district works differently. Taxes on growth above the "TIF Base" flow to the TIF fund rather than the other taxing bodies. The Treasurer gives the formula as (Net Taxable Value minus TIF Base) times the Tax Rate. The county doesn't create TIF districts or control how the money is spent.

Late penalties and the tax sale

Illinois law has the collector add a 1.5% penalty for each month an installment is late, and an installment is timely only if paid on or before its due date. Unpaid tax goes to the annual tax sale.

Franklin County tax and appeal rules at a glance
RuleAmount or timing

Board of Review startConvenes the first Monday in June

Evidence for unequal treatment5 comparable properties with size, age and condition

Bidders at the sale pay the taxes and penalties, then charge the owner interest. If the owner doesn't repay the buyer in the allowed time, the buyer may ask a court for a deed. Separately, the county takes sealed bids on real estate and mobile homes it has acquired for delinquent taxes, and a delinquent tax agent runs a yearly sale of those parcels.

How to contest an assessment

You can begin with the township assessor or go straight to the Board of Review, and each has its own time frame. The Board accepts complaints in writing, on its own forms, signed and showing the property address, within 30 calendar days after the assessment list is published for the year in question.

Put all your evidence in with the original complaint, since the Board looks only at what it receives. A claim of overvaluation needs proof such as an appraisal. A claim of unequal treatment needs five comparable properties nearby, with square footage, age and condition for each.

If the Board's ruling doesn't satisfy you, the next stop is the Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board. The Treasurer adds that a taxpayer with a dispute left after the complaint process can go to circuit court, but has to keep paying the billed tax meanwhile to avoid tax liens. Keep a copy of everything you file.

Homestead and other exemptions

Most exemptions require a residential home that the taxpayer owns and lives in. The Supervisor of Assessments lists these programs:

  • General homestead exemption for owner-occupied single-family homes
  • Senior citizens homestead exemption for owners 65 and older
  • Senior assessment freeze, which needs Form PTAX-340 filed every year
  • Homestead improvement exemption, covering four years after an improvement is finished and occupied
  • Disabled persons exemption, filed on PTAX-343 and renewed each year with PTAX-343-R
  • Disabled veteran standard and homestead exemptions
  • Returning veteran exemption, on Form PTAX-341

Dollar amounts change nearly every year, so ask the assessment office for current figures. Only the general homestead and senior homestead exemptions skip annual renewal. Seniors can also use the county's real estate tax deferral through the Treasurer, which places a lien on the home and is repaid when it sells or transfers. The state's Circuit Breaker grant is applied for through the Illinois Department of Revenue.

Franklin County housing at a glance

Franklin County is in Southern Illinois. Benton is the seat, and West Frankfort is the largest city. Population is 36,916 and there are 18,461 housing units. The median owner-occupied home is valued at $89,000, and 74.1% of housing units are owner-occupied. Median household income is $56,740 and median gross rent is $803. Building activity is slow, with just 19 permits issued in 2025.

Selling a Franklin County house

The bill is mailed to the owner at the address on the deed. In a typical transaction the seller credits the buyer for real estate taxes at closing, and the two sides work that out between them.

Here's a sensible order of steps before you close:

  • Call the Treasurer for installment dates and the amount still owed on the parcel, since the bill itself carries the exact figures.
  • If taxes are unpaid, clear them before the sale date, because a delinquent house can be in line for the tax sale.
  • If the bill goes to an old address, return the county's change of address form to the Supervisor of Assessments.
  • Give the title company the exact balance so the closing statement is right.

Nothing in the county's process bars a sale while tax is owed. A cash sale just means the balance gets settled from proceeds at closing, without a lender's payoff step.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay property tax in Franklin County, Illinois?

Pay the Franklin County Treasurer at the Government Annex Building, 901 Public Square in Benton, or by mail to PO Box 967. The office phone is 618-435-9800, and the county website has a real estate tax inquiry link.

What is the late penalty for Franklin County property tax?

It's 1.5% per month on each late installment, as Illinois law requires. An installment is on time only if it's paid by its due date, and unpaid tax can be sold at the annual tax sale.

How much interest can a Franklin County tax buyer charge?

A winning bidder at the tax sale charges the owner interest at an initial maximum rate of 18%. If the buyer pays later years' taxes too, the initial rate on those is 12%.

Who hears assessment complaints in Franklin County?

The Board of Review, which has three citizen members appointed by the County Board. Complaints are due within 30 calendar days after the assessment list is published, and Board rulings can be appealed to the Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board.

Can I sell my Franklin County house if the tax is unpaid?

Yes. Buyer and seller settle the tax at closing, and nothing bars a sale. Call the Treasurer for the exact balance first so the closing statement carries the right figure.

Who handles property tax in Fulton County

Three offices are involved. The Treasurer, who is also the ex-officio County Collector, sends the bills and takes payment. The Supervisor of Assessments oversees values and exemptions. The Board of Review hears assessment complaints, and the Supervisor of Assessments serves as its clerk. Both main offices are in the Fulton County Courthouse, 100 N. Main Street, Lewistown. Canton, Cuba, Farmington, Lewistown and Astoria are all billed by the same Treasurer.

  • Treasurer/Collector: PO Box 111, Lewistown, IL 61542; (309) 547-3041, extension 132; counter open 8:00 am to 4:00 pm weekdays
  • Supervisor of Assessments: PO Box 283, same courthouse; same main number, extension 113; no lunch closure
  • Township assessors set values in townships that have one. In the rest, county deputy assessors do the yearly fieldwork.

Fulton County housing at a glance

Fulton County is in west central Illinois, with Lewistown as the seat and Canton as the largest city. It's a lower-priced market with a shrinking population: 32,901 residents, 2.3% fewer than the 2020 base, in 15,869 housing units. Owners live in 76.6% of the homes. The typical owner-occupied home is worth $107,200, median gross rent is $785 and median household income is $60,599. At those values, an unpaid tax bill or a long repair list takes a bigger bite out of a sale price than it would in a costlier market.

How a Fulton County tax bill is figured

The formula on the Treasurer's bill insert is simple: equalized assessed value (EAV), minus exemptions, times the total local tax rate equals the bill. EAV is typically 33 1/3% of fair market value, adjusted by a state-mandated multiplier. School districts, the county, municipalities, townships and special districts such as park, library, fire protection and sanitary districts all take a share. Distributions to those taxing bodies go out every 30 days from the first due date.

Fulton County bills a year behind. Taxes on the 2024 assessment were mailed in 2025, with the first installment due June 13 and the second September 5. Each bill carries two payment stubs. Read the dates on your current bill, because a bill that never arrived is still owed.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Fulton County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Ways to pay

The Treasurer takes payment in person, by mail, at most county banks, in a courthouse drop box, online and by phone. The counter accepts cash, personal checks, cashier's checks, money orders and cards, and cards carry a convenience fee. Each channel stops working at a different point in the year, which matters if a closing date slips.

Fulton County payment channels and cutoffs
ChannelHours or cutoff
Courthouse counterMonday to Friday, 8:00 am to 4:00 pm; bring the stubs
MailMust be postmarked on time; a postage meter imprint is not accepted as proof
