Kankakee County in brief

The city of Kankakee is both the seat and the largest city of Kankakee County, which lies south of Will County along the Kankakee River. Only Kankakee and Momence are cities, so most homes here are in villages, townships and rural areas. There are seventeen townships, and the county publishes a directory of township assessors. The valuation behind your tax bill starts at the township level.

Population is about 105,525, down 2.0 percent from the April 2020 base. The county has 45,655 housing units and 40,996 households. Owners live in 69.9 percent of homes, and the typical owner-occupied home is worth $192,600. Owners report $1,649 a month in costs with a mortgage and $718 without. Median household income is $71,281.

Who to call

Four bodies matter: the township assessor, the Supervisor of Assessments, the County Treasurer and the Board of Review. The Supervisor of Assessments and the Treasurer both work from 189 East Court Street in Kankakee, IL 60901.

Kankakee County property tax offices
OfficeRoleContact
Township assessorsValuation of each parcelDirectory on the Supervisor of Assessments page
Supervisor of AssessmentsHomestead exemptions, parcel roll, transfer declarations, equalization, notice of assessment changes(815) 937-2945, weekdays
Board of ReviewAppeals, non-homestead exemption recommendations, omitted propertyThrough the Supervisor of Assessments, who serves as its clerk
County TreasurerBilling and collection(815) 937-2960, weekdays

The Treasurer's office manages about 55,760 property accounts and about $257 million in annual collections. Spanish-speaking staff are at the counter.

Due dates and penalties

Bills are payable in two installments, one in June and one in early September, and the Treasurer posts the exact dates each year. The taxes in each bill relate to the previous assessment year, so a bill payable this year reflects finalized assessed values from the year before.

Late payments carry a penalty of 1.5 percent per month, matching 35 ILCS 200/21-15 for a county with fewer than 3,000,000 residents. The Treasurer's calendar also sets a cutoff for paying by personal check without a newspaper publication fee, a mailing of delinquent notices, and a last day to pay in the office. The annual tax sale of delinquent properties takes place each November. Ask the Treasurer for the dates that apply to your bill.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Kankakee County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Spreading out payments

The Treasurer runs a voluntary program called CHOICES that lets an owner prepay weekly or monthly instead of waiting for the two due dates. It suits owners without mortgage escrow, and skipping a planned payment brings no penalty.

Fees are $1 per electronic check and 2.25 percent plus $1.50 for credit cards. Pay online, by mail, or in person at the Treasurer's office or its drop box, but not at a bank. The program does not stop the 1.5 percent monthly charge on a balance left after a due date, and each full installment must be paid by its date to avoid interest. Paying early earns no discount. If you sell mid-year, ask the Treasurer how your prepayments will be applied to the current bill.

How to appeal your assessment

Speak to your township assessor first. Then file the county's Assessment Appeal Form with the Kankakee County Board of Review. The Supervisor of Assessments page lists the publication and appeal deadlines, the Board of Review rules and procedures, and the form itself.

The Board sets the assessed value of an appealed parcel based on evidence presented at a public hearing. Deadlines run from the publication date of each township's assessment changes, and those dates differ across the seventeen townships, so look up yours before you plan. The Supervisor of Assessments at (815) 937-2945 can give you the date that applies to your parcel.

Exemptions

The Supervisor of Assessments office has applications for homestead relief, and exemptions must be filed by March 1 each year. Senior and disability exemptions go through the assessor.

  • General and Senior Homestead Exemptions, with a combined application.
  • Senior Assessment Freeze, form PTAX-340, with a separate form for each tax year.
  • Disabled Person (PTAX-343) and the Physician's Statement (PTAX-343-A), plus an application for a Disabled Person ID Card.
  • Disabled veteran (PTAX-342) and returning veteran exemptions.
  • Homestead Improvements, for added value from a new improvement.

Dollar limits are printed on the county forms, so open the form for the exemption you want before you count on a reduction.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Kankakee County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Storm damage and the disaster exemption

Bills are based on the prior year's assessed values, so damage from a storm this year cannot lower the bill now due. The assessor can still review a damaged home. If your house is damaged or uninhabitable, contact the township assessor or the Supervisor of Assessments so the property is reviewed for the current tax year.

The Natural Disaster Homestead Exemption under 35 ILCS 200/15-173 may apply after the structure is rebuilt. The county lists these requirements:

  • The structure must be rebuilt within two years of the disaster.
  • The rebuilt square footage may not exceed 110 percent of the original.
  • The first application is due no later than the first taxable year after the rebuild.
  • The exemption must be applied for each year.

A house with deferred repairs or storm damage should have its tax and exemption status checked before you list it, so a buyer's inspection does not turn up a surprise.

Getting ready to list

Begin with the Treasurer's account for your parcel and confirm what is paid and what is open. Then ask the Supervisor of Assessments which exemptions are on file, because a buyer's lender or title company will ask. Collect your last bill, your assessment notice and any exemption forms in one folder. If you use the CHOICES program, print your payment history so the closing agent can credit what you prepaid. When the house sits in a township you are unsure of, the directory on the Supervisor's page names the assessor to call.

Plan the timing of your listing against the tax calendar too. A closing that lands between the first and second installment means the buyer and seller must agree on who covers the bill, and the contract should say so in plain words.

Selling with taxes owed

Get a payoff figure from the Treasurer at (815) 937-2960 and confirm which installments are paid. Taxes unpaid at the November sale can be offered at that sale, so a sale of the house should not wait past that date with a balance still open. The title company can settle the balance from your proceeds at closing. A cash sale skips a lender's underwriting, which leaves tax and title checks as the main items to clear before closing.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay property tax?

Pay the County Treasurer at 189 East Court Street in Kankakee, phone (815) 937-2960. The counter is open on weekdays.

What does a late payment cost?

Late installments accrue interest at 1.5 percent per month. Taxes still owing at the annual November tax sale can be offered at that sale.

Where do seniors apply for relief?

Apply through the Supervisor of Assessments at (815) 937-2945. Exemption filings are due by March 1 each year, and the county posts the senior, disabled person and disabled veteran forms.

Can I appeal my assessment?

Yes. Speak to your township assessor first, then file the county's assessment appeal form with the Board of Review within the deadline listed for your township.

Is there help with storm damage on my house?

Contact your township assessor or the Supervisor of Assessments so the property can be reviewed for the current tax year. The natural disaster exemption may apply once the home is rebuilt, within two years and no more than 110 percent of the original size.

Kendall County at a glance

Kendall County is a quickly growing Chicago-area county. Yorkville is the seat and Oswego has the most people. Homes cluster in the northeast and by the Fox River, and the south is mostly farms. Who handles property tax

  • Township assessor: explains how your assessment was determined. The phone number is on the back of the tax bill.
  • Supervisor of Assessments, (630) 553-4146: assessment, property description, multiplier and exemption questions, and clerk to the Board of Review.
  • County Clerk, (630) 553-4104: tax rates and tax levies.
  • County Collector (Treasurer), (630) 553-4124: billing and payment.

Need a different name or mailing address on the bill? Mail a Change of Address form to the assessment office. Doing this before you sell keeps the final bill from going to the wrong place.

How assessments work

Property other than farmland is assessed at a 33.33 percent median level of fair cash value. The 2026 valuation date was January 1, 2026, using sales from 2023, 2024 and 2025. The bill itself comes from equalized assessed value, less exemptions, times the current rate.

Nine townships make up the county: Big Grove, Bristol, Fox, Kendall, Lisbon, Little Rock, Na-Au-Say, Oswego and Seward. Equalization factors are applied so each township reaches the required level.

Kendall County 2026 equalization by township
TownshipCurrent median ratioEqualization factor
Big Grove31.60%1.0547
Bristol33.33%1.0000
Fox33.33%1.0000
Kendall33.33%1.0000
Lisbon33.33%1.0000
Little Rock33.33%1.0000

To test for over-assessment, divide your assessment by the median level of assessment. If the result is above the estimated fair cash value, you may be over-assessed.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Kendall County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to appeal your assessment

Start with your township assessor, then file a written complaint with the Board of Review. The window closes on the 30th day after publication for your township, and the filing date changes each year.

Three people sit on the Board of Review, appointed by the County Board, and each one passes a state exam. They look over what township assessors did, pick up omitted property, hear complaints and may change an assessment on their own motion. They also even out the townships and review exemption petitions, then pass the final valuations to the County Clerk, who computes tax rates. Complaint forms, instructions and the board's rules are available by calling (630) 553-4146.

Billing and late payment

You get a single bill in May with two equal installments. Nothing is mailed when the second one falls due. Interest of 1.5 percent a month runs on any installment left unpaid past its due date.

  • A bill that never arrives still has to be paid, and penalties still apply.
  • A $10.00 fee is added to the delinquent notice mailed after the second installment.
  • The minimum charge for a bounced check is $25.00, and the payment is voided.
  • The county does not mail the original bill to a mortgage company, so check with your lender about getting a copy.
  • A duplicate bill is free to the owner, and non-owners pay $5.00.

A payment made on the wrong parcel cannot be refunded automatically. Ask the Collector at (630) 553-4124 for the installment dates printed on your bill.

Paying under protest

Protesting means paying everything first, then filing a tax objection complaint with the Kendall County Circuit Clerk. That makes the payment one made under protest, and you do not need to mark the bill or fill in a protest form when you pay.

Two clocks run from the first penalty date of the second installment. Full payment is due by day 60, and the complaint by day 75. The Circuit Clerk's fee is $119.00 for the first parcel and $50.00 for each added parcel. An objection to the assessed value requires that you first filed an assessment complaint with the Board of Review, and a filing with the state Property Tax Appeal Board for the same year blocks it. The county tax sale has generally been held in late October, so full payment must come before the sale to keep a property off it.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Kendall County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Homestead and other exemptions

The assessment office lists homestead programs, and a driver's license must show the property address to receive any homestead exemption. Ask the office for current amounts before relying on any figure.

  • General Homestead Exemption: up to $6,000 on the increase above the 1977 value. Apply once while ownership and residency stay the same.
  • Home Improvement Exemption: up to $75,000 of added value for four years, certified by the township assessor with no application.
  • Senior Citizen Homestead Exemption: a $5,000 reduction for owners 65 or older, with a yearly renewal form mailed by the office.
  • Senior Assessment Freeze: household income cap of $65,000, yearly application, due on or before September 1.
  • Returning veteran exemption: a $5,000 reduction for two consecutive years.
  • Disabled veteran standard exemption: $2,500 for a 30 to 49 percent rating, $5,000 for 50 to 69 percent, and the first $250,000 of assessed value exempt at 70 percent or more.
  • Disabled Persons: a $2,000 reduction, with an annual application.

Religious, charitable and educational groups apply for non-homestead exemption through the Board of Review.

Before you list

Search your parcel in the county's online tax bill lookup to see the amount owed, and ask the Collector at (630) 553-4124 to confirm what is unpaid. If you owe back tax, the payoff comes out of your proceeds at the closing table. A cash sale skips a lender's underwriting, so the tax and title checks are usually what decide the closing date. Tell the title company about any protest in progress, since a tax paid under protest can still be settled at closing.

Frequently asked questions

Which Kendall County office collects the tax?

The Kendall County Collector bills and collects, at 504 S. Main St in Yorkville, phone (630) 553-4124. Tax rate and levy questions go to the County Clerk at (630) 553-4104.

How is the tax split into installments?

One bill is mailed in May and payable in two equal installments. No second bill is sent, and unpaid installments accrue 1.5 percent interest per month.

When is the deadline to appeal an assessment?

Complaints must be filed in writing with the Board of Review within 30 days after your township's publication. Call (630) 553-4146 for the date this year.

Can I pay Kendall County taxes under protest?

Yes. Pay the full tax within 60 days of the second installment's first penalty date and file a tax objection complaint with the Circuit Clerk within 75 days. The Clerk's fee is $119.00 for the first parcel.

Is there a senior freeze?

Yes, for owners 65 and up whose household income is $65,000 or less. The county wants the application by September 1 every year.

Knox County, IL Property Tax Guide: Offices, Appeals and Selling With Tax Due

Cash Home Buyers in Illinois
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Knox County, IL Property Tax Guide: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Who handles property tax

A seller in Knox County will typically deal with three offices. The County Treasurer, in the courthouse in Galesburg, mails the bills and takes the money. The county Assessment Office, 309-345-3845, runs exemptions and hands out Board of Review forms. Township assessors set the values. Tax sale certificates and redemption sit with the County Clerk.

Assessing is split three ways. One assessor covers the North District: Rio, Ontario, Walnut Grove, Lynn, Henderson, Sparta, Copley, Victoria, Persifer and Truro townships. Another covers the South District: Galesburg, Knox, Cedar, Orange, Haw Creek, Elba, Indian Point, Chestnut, Maquon and Salem. The City of Galesburg township has its own assessor, so the right call depends on where the parcel sits.

Knox County homes and prices

Galesburg is both the seat and the biggest city of Knox County, in west central Illinois. Population is sliding, from 49,967 in the 2020 count to an estimated 47,767 in July 2025. The median home value is $111,900, 70.8% of households own their homes, and median income is $57,030.

Where values are this low, even a modest bill takes a real share of a house's worth, so look at the assessment before you list.

Due dates and penalties

Taxes are payable in two installments, around July 1 and September 1. Knox County mails one bill a year with a detachable stub for each installment, so read the dates on your current bill or ask the Treasurer.

Knox County late penalty by date
Penalty startsFirst installmentSecond installment
July 21.50%Not yet due
August 23.00%Not yet due
September 24.50%1.50%
October 26.00%3.00%
November 27.50%4.50%

The charge is 1.5% each month, applies in full rather than by the day, and begins the morning after a due date. A bill that never arrives does not excuse the tax (35 ILCS 200/20-15).

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Knox County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Where to pay

The Treasurer takes payment several ways, and the detachable stub has to go with it:

  • Mail a check or deliver it to the Treasurer's Office, made out to Knox County Collector. A mailed check's cancelled copy is your receipt.
  • Leave a check in a courthouse drop box, one on Tompkins Street by the north curb and one at the parking lot exit. No envelopes are supplied.
  • Take it to a local bank in the county (Wells Fargo is excluded at its own request).
  • Use a credit or debit card and pay a fee of 2.35%, with a $2.95 minimum.

A postmark counts if the payment goes out before the tax sale. Drop box items collected at 8:30 each morning are posted to the day before. If a lender pays from escrow, the county still expects the owner to watch those payments.

How assessments are set

Assessors value property as of each January 1, aiming for 33.33% of fair cash value and drawing on three years of sales. Equalization factors follow. For 2026 they were 1.0724 in Galesburg Township, 1.0758 for the City of Galesburg, 1.0132 in Rio, Walnut Grove, Henderson and Persifer, and 1.0125 in Ontario, Sparta and Copley. Lynn, Truro, Victoria, Elba and Salem were general assessment townships that year.

The formula for a bill takes the final equalized assessed value, subtracts exemptions, and multiplies what remains by the tax rate. To test your own figure, divide the assessment by 0.3333 and compare that with a realistic sale price.

Before the 2026 adjustments, the three-year median assessment level measured 32.92% in the North District, 31.08% in the South District and 31.76% in the City of Galesburg, which is why the factors push values upward. Farmland follows a separate state formula, and its factor was 1.00.

How to appeal your assessment

Talk to the township assessor first. If that does not settle it, put a written appeal in front of the Board of Review. It must argue the property's value, not the size of the tax. The filing period opens in mid-September and closes in the second half of October, ending at 4 p.m. on the last day. Each year brings new forms, and older ones are refused.

  • Support the appeal with facts, such as an independent appraisal or sales of comparable homes.
  • The Board answers with a notice carrying an informal decision.
  • To contest it, return your acceptance of a formal hearing within ten days of the notice.
  • Thirty days after a final Board decision is the limit for going to the Property Tax Appeal Board.

The Board of Review meets as needed rather than on a fixed calendar. For the current forms and window, call the Assessment Office at 309-345-3845.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Knox County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Exemptions

Exemption forms and instructions are on the county's assessment pages, and the Treasurer's page summarizes the main ones:

  • Owner-occupied homestead: a reduction of up to $6,000 in equalized assessed value.
  • Senior homestead for owners 65 and older: $5,000 off.
  • Senior assessment freeze: holds the taxable value for owners 65 and older. The Treasurer lists household income of $65,000 or less, and the assessment office shows $75,000 for 2026.
  • Home improvement: assessed value of up to $25,000 exempt for four years.

Other exemptions cover returning veteran, disabled person and disabled veteran cases. Applications are requested by September 30 each year and accepted until December 31. A buyer who moves in should contact the assessment office after the next January 1 to confirm the exemption is on the parcel.

Delinquent taxes and the tax sale

Knox County runs one tax sale a year, usually in mid-November, and every delinquent tax is offered. A list of delinquent taxes is printed in local newspapers each mid-October. Under Public Act 104-0553, the county now acquires all delinquent real estate taxes itself as trustee for the taxing districts. That trustee then auctions parcels it has taken to deed.

Tax sale certificates are handled by the County Clerk's Office, 309-345-6753. The Treasurer will not give legal advice about delinquent taxes.

Selling with taxes owed

If tax is outstanding when you sell, ask the Treasurer what is owed and settle it at closing from your proceeds. Have the title company confirm with the Clerk that no certificate has been issued on the parcel. A cash sale skips a lender's underwriting, so these two checks are often what set the closing date. For a buyer who plans to live in the house, remind them to ask the assessment office about the homestead exemption after the next January 1, because it does not carry over automatically.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

What dates does Knox County collect real estate tax?

Taxes come due in two installments, around July 1 and September 1. The Treasurer mails one annual bill with a stub for each installment, so read the dates on your own bill.

What late fee does Knox County charge?

The Treasurer adds 1.5% per month to the unpaid amount, with no proration, starting the day after a due date.

When can I appeal my assessment?

The Board of Review filing period opens in mid-September and closes in the second half of October, and the Board may not accept complaints afterward. Call the Assessment Office at 309-345-3845 for the current window.

Where do I send a property tax payment?

The Treasurer's Office in the Knox County courthouse in Galesburg takes mail and walk-in payments. Drop boxes, most local banks and card payments are also options, and checks go to the Knox County Collector.

When does Knox County hold the tax sale?

It is usually held in mid-November, following a mid-October newspaper list of delinquent taxes. The County Clerk handles the certificates.

Cash Home Buyers in Illinois

Selling in Lake County?

Who does what on property tax

Lake County property tax runs through several offices, each with its own job. The Treasurer (847-377-2323) mails the bills, collects payment and passes the money to the districts. The Chief County Assessment Office supervises values, with township assessors doing the local work. Appeals go to the Board of Review. The County Clerk works out the rates and takes over after a tax sale for redemption.

The county has 18 townships, and your township assessor is the place to start with a worry about the number on your assessment notice. Little of what you pay stays with county government, which gets about seven percent of an average bill. School districts take about 69 percent. More than 200 separate taxing bodies levy tax here, so the mix depends on the parcel. The bill itself shows which ones apply.

Lake County homes and costs

Lake County fills the northeast corner of Illinois, with Waukegan as seat and largest city. Population is about 719,339. The median home value is $345,700, owners live in 74.8% of homes, and median household income is $110,416. Owners with a mortgage report median monthly costs of $2,503, so a tax bill of several thousand dollars a year is a real line item for a buyer.

How the tax cycle works

One cycle spans two years, so a bill reflects work done the year before. In year one, township assessors set values as of January 1 at one third of fair market value, using three years of sales. The county equalizes values across townships, mails assessment notices known as blue sheets, and the Board of Review hears appeals. Taxing districts pass budgets and levies the same year.

In year two, the Board finishes its hearings, the County Clerk figures tax rates from the levies and the final values, and the Treasurer mails bills at the start of May. By the time the bill arrives, it is too late to protest it. The time to speak up is at the assessment notice and at the budget meetings of the taxing districts.

Due dates and the tax calendar

Bills arrive in early May, with installments in June and September. The Treasurer's calendar follows this sequence, and the exact dates are posted each year:

Lake County real estate tax calendar
EventUsual date

Last day to pay to avoid tax sale, by 5:00 p.m., no postmarkNovember 12
Tax saleNovember 13

Due dates, interest dates and the tax sale date are fixed. Other dates on the calendar may shift for administrative reasons.

Late penalties and prepaying

Under state law the collector adds 1.5% a month to any unpaid installment, figured on the 5th of the month with no proration. A first installment paid between June 5 and July 4 carries 1.5%, and by the October 5 to November 12 window it reaches 7.5%. The second installment starts at 1.5% on September 5 and reaches 3.0% in the last window.

  • Not receiving a bill, medical emergencies and travel do not qualify for forgiveness of the penalty.
  • Forgiveness applies only to a documented Lake County error.
  • In the final weeks before the sale, the Treasurer's Office takes only cash or certified funds, in person.
  • A December prepayment window lets owners pay up to 50% of the previous year's bill, by check only, with the parcel number in the memo line.

Owners who pay through mortgage escrow can look up status on the Treasurer's site by parcel number, though a payment can take weeks to appear as paid.

How to appeal your assessment

Each township has its own deadline, which falls one month after its assessments are published. Final filing dates run from late August in the earliest townships to early November in the latest, and a missed window forfeits the appeal for that year. Ask the Chief County Assessment Office for your township's date as soon as the notice arrives.

The Board urges a conversation with the township assessor beforehand and requires one for factual-error appeals. Appeals are filed online through the Smartfile system. The county names these reasons as typical:

  • A factual error such as the wrong square footage
  • An assessment above one third of the recent sale price
  • An assessment above one third of market value
  • An assessment higher than comparable properties

You may choose a hearing by letter, phone, in person or Zoom, and corporations and LLCs must use an attorney. Hearings are finished in early February.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Lake County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Homestead and other exemptions

Exemptions are filed through the Smartfile e-filing portal run by the Chief County Assessment Office, and staff will help by phone or in person.

  • General homestead: takes $8,000 off equalized assessed value for an owner's main residence as of January 1, with no yearly renewal.
  • Senior exemption: another $8,000, which can be claimed on top of the general homestead.
  • Senior assessment freeze: protects limited-income seniors from increases from rising values, but not from higher tax rates.
  • Senior tax deferral: lets qualified seniors defer part or all of the tax on their residence.
  • Home improvement, disabled persons and veteran exemptions.

Exemptions do not transfer to a newly assigned parcel number, so a split or combined lot needs a fresh application under the new number.

The tax sale and selling with taxes owed

By law the Treasurer sells each year's unpaid taxes, and the sale falls in November after the October final notices. The house itself is not sold, just the delinquent taxes. A tax buyer pays them, the districts receive the money, and the owner then works with the County Clerk's Office on redemption.

A seller who owes tax should clear it by closing. The Treasurer can quote the amount due, and the County Clerk can estimate redemption for a parcel already sold. The Treasurer's Office also handles payment status, delinquent prior-year taxes and duplicate bills. A cash sale skips a lender's underwriting, so the payoff and title check are the main steps left before closing.

Before you list, pull the parcel number from your bill and look up its payment status on the Treasurer's site. Gather your assessment notice and any exemption confirmation too. If a payment is made close to the sale, remember that escrow payments can take weeks to show as paid, so keep proof of payment handy for the title company. Ask the buyer's side early how the year's tax will be split, since the bill you receive in May reflects the prior year.

Frequently asked questions

What are the property tax due dates?

Bills are mailed in early May with installments in June and September. The Treasurer posts the exact dates each year, and the tax sale date is fixed in November.

How much is the penalty on a late payment?

State law adds 1.5% per month to an unpaid installment, counted on the 5th and never prorated. Forgiveness is limited to documented Lake County errors.

What is the deadline to contest an assessment?

One month after your township's assessments are published. Dates run from late August to early November depending on the township.

Does Lake County sell the house at the tax sale?

No. Only the unpaid taxes are sold, and the owner then redeems through the County Clerk's Office.

Is there a way to prepay property tax?

Yes, during a December window announced by the Treasurer. Prepayment may be up to 50% of the prior year's bill, by check only, with the parcel number in the memo.

Selling in Lee County?

Lee County offices for tax questions

The work is split among four offices in Dixon. Ask the assessment staff about value or exemptions, bring payment trouble to the Treasurer, and take rate-calculation questions to the Clerk's extension department.

Lee County offices that touch a property tax bill
OfficeWhat it handlesPhone and location
Treasurer and CollectorPrints and collects bills, runs the annual tax sale, administers senior deferral815-288-4477, 112 E Second Street, mailing box 328
Chief County Assessment OfficeValues, exemptions, appeal paperwork815-288-4483, open weekdays from 8 until 4:30
Board of ReviewDecides assessment complaints815-288-4483, first floor of the old courthouse
County Clerk and RecorderExtends rates, takes redemption money after a sale, records deeds815-288-3309, mailing box 329

The Treasurer collects more than $96 million this year and passes it to over 130 taxing districts. That is why a Lee County bill reads like a ledger of school, township, fire and county lines instead of a single charge.

Lee County at a glance

Population is 32,914 as of July 2025, down from 34,145 in 2020. About 73.6% of occupied homes have owners living in them. The midpoint value for an owner-occupied home is $154,600, and builders took out just 32 permits in 2025, so resale buyers have few new houses to compare against. Dixon is the seat and the biggest city. An EF4 tornado touched down in the county on April 9, 2015, so expect a buyer to ask about storm history.

Several school districts cut across the county, including Dixon Unit 170, Amboy 272, Ashton 275, Lee Center 271, Polo 222 and Sterling 5. Whichever one serves your address drives much of your rate.

How Lee County values a home

Township assessors propose values, and the county assessment office pulls them together. Houses are assessed at one-third of fair cash value. If a single parcel changes, the office mails you a notice. If the only change is a township-wide equalization factor, no notice is required.

Illinois runs on a four-year general reassessment. For 2026 the townships in their general year are Amboy, Ashton, Bradford, Franklin Grove, Nachusa, Lee Center, May and Sublette. You can look over a parcel's size, age, lot and sketch at the assessment counter, or search property record cards on the county site.

A bigger bill does not always mean a bigger assessment. Usually one of three things happened: a taxing district asked for more, an exemption you qualify for was never applied, or other owners picked up exemptions you lack. Under the state's extension limitation law, most districts may grow their levy by the smaller of 5% or inflation over the highest of the prior three years. New construction, bonds and referendum-approved increases sit outside that cap.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Lee County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to appeal your assessment

Your written complaint has to reach the Board of Review within 30 calendar days of the date the list is published (35 ILCS 200/16-55). For the townships named above, the publication date is November 18, 2026 and the last day to file is December 18, 2026. Other townships have their own publication dates, so ask the assessment staff which one applies to you.

The Board has three members chosen by the County Board. It may confirm, lower or raise a value. These grounds are accepted:

  • Equity, meaning your value is out of line with similar homes
  • Fair cash value
  • A wrong physical description of the property
  • Questions of law

Before filing, try your township assessor or county staff, because many disputes are settled in that conversation. After the 30 days, only a physical-data mismatch, such as a house recorded larger than it is, can still be raised. If you dislike the Board's ruling, the Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board is the next step, at 217-782-6076 or 401 S Spring Street, Room 402, Springfield. It looks at value only, so a complaint about the size of the final bill belongs with the taxing districts.

Due dates and how to pay

The bill comes in two installments, and the county prints each due date on the bill. Under 35 ILCS 200/21-15, the first installment is late once the later of June 1 or the day after the printed date goes by. The second installment uses the same test with September 1. Each month or part of a month that you are late adds interest of 1 1/2%. Mail with a postmark on or before the date is treated as timely.

Ways to pay:

  • The county's property tax inquiry website, which shows a pay link after you search by PIN, owner name or address.
  • Phone payment at 877-690-3729 with jurisdiction code 7042.
  • A check mailed to Lee County Collector, P.O. Box 328, Dixon, IL 61021.
  • The Treasurer's counter at the Old Lee County Courthouse.

Card payments carry a 2.40% fee through a third party, with a $2.00 minimum. E-checks cost $2 up to $50,000, then $4, $8.50 and $10 in higher bands. A bill that never showed up still has to be paid, so ask the Treasurer for a copy. Send address updates on the county's change-of-address form.

Exemptions that lower a bill

Each exemption comes off your equalized assessed value ahead of the tax rate. Because no county with 3,000,000 or more residents touches Lee, the smaller statutory caps are the ones in force. Here are the common ones:

  • General homestead: up to $6,000 off a house you occupy as your main residence (35 ILCS 200/15-175).
  • Senior citizens: up to $5,000 off, starting in the assessment year you turn 65 (35 ILCS 200/15-170). Once approved it carries forward by itself, but you must notify the office if the home no longer qualifies.
  • Senior freeze: a yearly application, with household income kept under the limit on the county form.
  • Tax deferral: the Treasurer's program for owners 65 and over whose household income is at most $75,000, moving to $77,000 for tax year 2026 and $79,000 for 2027. The postponed tax stays as a lien until the house sells.

File exemption forms with the assessment office. After a sale, state law keeps the seller's homestead credit through the assessment year of the sale, and the office can ask the buyer to apply for the following year.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Lee County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with taxes owed

The thing auctioned at a tax sale is the delinquent tax, never the house itself. Each year the Treasurer puts every unpaid parcel into the sale. You can redeem by paying the tax with costs and interest. Redemption is handled at the County Clerk's office.

The redemption window generally runs three years from the sale, though 35 ILCS 200/21-350 carves out exceptions. When someone already holds a certificate on your parcel, ask the Clerk for the payoff amount and last day in writing before pricing the house or signing anything.

Property taxes at a Lee County closing

The title agent or closing attorney pulls the most recent bill, looks for open installments, and splits the tax year between you and the buyer on the settlement statement. Ahead of that, ask the Treasurer if an earlier year is delinquent or sold, because any such balance gets paid out of your proceeds. With an escrow account, find out which installments the lender has already sent in.

Houses that come with probate, tenants or deferred repairs often carry back taxes too. Get a payoff letter from the Treasurer, and a redemption figure from the Clerk if a sale took place, so every offer is measured against the same debt. A cash buyer can close on those figures without waiting for a lender's review.

Frequently asked questions

Which number reaches the Lee County Treasurer?

815-288-4477 for bills and payments. The assessment office at 815-288-4483 takes value, exemption and appeal questions, and the Clerk's extension department at 815-288-3309 explains how rates are built and handles redemption.

Can I still appeal late in Lee County?

Only when the county's record describes the house wrongly, for instance the wrong square footage. Every other complaint has a 30-day window that opens when the roll is published.

What is the largest general homestead reduction in Lee County?

$6,000 off equalized assessed value. That is the lower cap, since Lee borders no county of 3,000,000 or more people. Apply at the assessment office (35 ILCS 200/15-175).

What does late payment cost in Lee County?

It adds 1 1/2% for every month or part of one (35 ILCS 200/21-15). Late status begins after the statutory date or the day following the printed one, whichever is later, and a postmark on time prevents it.

Does Lee County's senior deferral wipe out the tax?

No. It postpones the tax, and the amount deferred is repaid from the sale price when the home is sold. You apply through the Treasurer and must be 65 or older.

Logan County housing snapshot

Logan County is central Illinois farm country. Lincoln is both the county seat and its largest city, and Atlanta and Mount Pulaski round out the list. I-55 links Lincoln to Bloomington and Springfield, and Amtrak stops at Lincoln Station. Land area is about 618 square miles.

Housing and income figures, Logan County
MeasureLogan County
Residents, July 2025 estimate27,182
Housing units, July 202511,941
Owner-occupied share68.5%
Median owner-occupied home value$134,400
Median monthly rent$829
Median household income$66,358
Building permits issued, 202564

Expect 126 freezing days a year, which is why inspectors on a Logan County house pay close attention to the roof, gutters and foundation.

Which county offices handle your tax bill

Three Lincoln offices split the job.

  • Supervisor of Assessments (122 N. McLean St., 217-732-9635): directs the township assessors, keeps tax maps and parcel record cards, grants exemptions and serves as clerk to the Board of Review.
  • County Clerk (courthouse Room 20, 217-732-4148): applies each levy to the assessed base to produce rates, and handles redemption of tax sale certificates.
  • County Treasurer (courthouse Room 11, 217-732-3761): mails bills, takes payments, logs granted appeals and distributes the money.

The Treasurer also serves as county collector for real estate, mobile home and drainage tax. Every owner pays county, township and road and bridge tax. Schools, fire protection and other districts add to that, so your rate depends on which boundaries enclose your parcel.

The yearly tax calendar

Billing runs a year behind: money collected in 2026 pays for tax year 2025. The same sequence returns every year.

  • Real estate bills are mailed in May.
  • Installment one is due June 15 and installment two September 1, and a missed one picks up a 1.5% penalty for each month.
  • Mobile home bills leave the office at the end of March, with payment due June 1. After that day a $25 penalty applies, and another $25 is added each month, capped at $100.
  • The annual tax sale takes place in the fall, and buyers must register about two weeks ahead.

Logan County has elected, under Public Act 104-0553, to take delinquent real estate taxes as trustee for the taxing districts. If you missed a due date, call the Treasurer for today's payoff, because the penalty grows monthly.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Logan County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Where to pay

Whichever way you pay, have the stub from your bill. The options:

  • The counter in courthouse Room 11, with cash or check. Real estate tax only can go on a card, which costs 2.35% plus $1.50.
  • The drop box on N. Kickapoo St. facing Latham Park, or the boxes on the north and south sides of the courthouse. No cash in the boxes.
  • Local banks, with the exception of Regions and CEFCU.
  • Mail, where the postmark counts as the date received.
  • Card or e-check by phone at 217-203-8359 with your property index number, or through the link on the Treasurer's web page.

Not receiving a bill does not excuse it. Under 35 ILCS 200/21-15 a postmark on or before the due date makes a mailed payment timely, and installment one is delinquent only after the later of June 1 or the day following the printed date.

How a Logan County bill is built

Township and county assessors set the assessed value. The abstract then goes to the state, which may apply a multiplier that raises, lowers or leaves values unchanged. For each district the County Clerk divides the levy by assessed valuation to get a rate, subject to any statutory cap. Multiply the combined rate by your equalized assessed value and you have the tax.

Homes are assessed at one-third of market value, and equalization factors from the Supervisor keep levels there. Board of Review rules set a four-year reassessment cycle for each parcel, with yearly reassessment permitted. Each year's assessment changes are published in the Lincoln Courier.

Mobile home registration also runs through the Supervisor. The title must be valid and taxes current, and moving a title at the Secretary of State takes a tax certificate from the Treasurer.

How to appeal your assessment

The deadline is 30 days after assessment changes for your township are published. Deliver the complaint and evidence to the assessment office before 4:30 p.m. that day, or mail them postmarked no later than it. Talking to the assessor does not pause the deadline.

Common stumbling blocks:

  • One complaint per parcel, on the Board's own form. Faxed and emailed complaints are refused.
  • Attach one copy of your evidence. Writing that no evidence is provided will probably bring a no-change decision.
  • You can contest the assessment but not the tax amount.
  • Missing items trigger a notice and 10 days to fix them.
  • Hearings are by appointment, last about 15 minutes, and take no new evidence.

The County Board appoints the Board of Review's three members, and the Board starts meeting by the first Monday of June. A written tentative decision comes to you, and a hearing request must be made inside the period shown on it.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Logan County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Homestead and other exemptions

Staff at the assessment office verify eligibility, and some exemptions need fresh proof yearly. What is available:

  • Owner-occupied homestead: $6,000 off assessed value when the owner lives in the house.
  • Senior citizen: a further $5,000 once the owner reaches 65, with proof of age.
  • Senior freeze: holds the value at the first qualifying year for owners already on the senior exemption, with household gross income of $65,000 or less in assessment year 2025 and $75,000 or less from 2026.
  • Homestead improvement: shelters the added value from a garage, porch or deck on an owner-occupied house for four years.
  • Returning service members: $5,000 off the main residence for two straight years.
  • Service-connected disability: $2,500 at a 30 to 49% rating, $5,000 at 50 to 69%, and full exemption at 70% or above.
  • Persons with disabilities: $2,000, renewed with annual proof.

The first two dollar amounts match the state statutes for counties not adjoining one of 3,000,000 or more (35 ILCS 200/15-175 and 15-170).

Selling with taxes owed

Search your parcel on the county tax lookup, match it to the bill in hand, and call the Treasurer about any open installment. At closing the title company prorates the year, and the settlement statement lists what is paid, owed or held in escrow. Your lender, if it escrows, can report what it has remitted.

Earlier years left unpaid complicate a sale. Find out from the County Clerk if the taxes were sold and what it costs to redeem, because whoever holds the certificate must be paid before title clears. Redemption generally lasts three years after the sale, subject to exceptions (35 ILCS 200/21-350). A cash buyer can close on the payoff numbers from those two offices, which keeps the schedule short when back taxes are involved.

Frequently asked questions

Which number reaches the Logan County Treasurer?

217-732-3761, for bill questions and past-due amounts. The office is in courthouse Room 11 in Lincoln.

How much is the late penalty in Logan County?

Real estate tax adds 1.5% per month after a missed due date. Mobile home tax adds $25 after June 1 and $25 each month more, up to $100.

Does the Logan County Treasurer accept cards?

For real estate tax, yes: at the counter, by phone at 217-203-8359 or online. The counter fee is 2.35% plus $1.50, and phone callers need the property index number.

What is the appeal window for a Logan County assessment?

Thirty days after your township's changes are published. File by 4:30 p.m. or postmark by that day, using a separate form for each parcel.

Where do I get the Logan County homestead exemption?

Contact the Supervisor of Assessments at 122 N. McLean St., Lincoln, 217-732-9635. The owner-occupied exemption is $6,000 off assessed value.

Paying Macon County property tax

Macon County is the Decatur area of central Illinois, and Decatur serves as the seat and the biggest city. The Treasurer mails roughly 55,000 bills a year, and the money funds schools, libraries, parks, cities and the county itself.

Find the Treasurer at 141 South Main Street, Room 302, in the Macon County Office Building in Decatur. The phone is 217-424-1426 and the hours are 8:30 to 4:30, Monday through Friday, closed legal holidays. Online payment runs through maconcountyil.us, and the payment site's help desk is 844-400-8880.

Macon County housing market numbers

Population was estimated at 99,300 on July 1, 2025, down 4.5% from April 2020. The county makes up the Decatur metropolitan area.

Macon County housing and income
MeasureMacon County
Households (2020-2024 survey)43,468
Housing units, July 202549,587
Owner-occupied share70.2%
Median owner-occupied home value$127,300
Median monthly rent$847

Building permits, 202538

With so few new homes built, most buyers here are shopping resale. January lows near 17 degrees make heating, roofing and drainage fair questions on any older house.

Who sets your value, and how to look it up

Down the hall at 141 South Main Street, Room 401, the Supervisor of Assessments answers at 217-424-1364 during the same weekday hours. That office supports the township assessors, runs exemptions, keeps parcel maps and record cards, applies equalization factors and publishes assessments in local papers. The Supervisor also serves as the Board of Review's clerk.

Outside Cook County, Illinois aims for 33 1/3% of market value. You can see your number on the county website, on a mailed notice if the parcel changed or the township is in its general year, in the newspaper publication, on your tax bill, or by phone. Property record cards print for $.35 a page by address or PIN. Sales transfer declarations can be viewed at the office, which helps if your appeal rests on comparable sales.

Your bill equals assessed value minus exemptions, times the rates of each district that serves the parcel. Homes a block apart can fall under different districts, so comparing with a neighbor's bill tells you little.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Macon County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to appeal your assessment

You get 30 calendar days counted from your assessment's publication, and townships publish on different dates. Ask the Supervisor's office for yours, since the statute allows no appeal once the deadline passes.

Three people appointed by the County Board make up the Board of Review. Between 800 and 1,000 appeals come before it in a tax year, and hearings typically finish by the end of February. Useful evidence includes:

  • A broker's market analysis
  • A certified appraisal
  • A grid of comparable properties
  • Your settlement statement from buying the house
  • Photos

You argue either equity, which compares assessments on similar nearby homes, or market value, which needs recent sales. The Board has no say over the tax bill, so a case built only on high taxes goes nowhere.

What follows a Board decision

The Board sits from June 1 and writes by mail only, so double-check the mailing address on your complaint. You will hear back in one of three ways. The Board may accept your numbers, offer its own tentative value with 10 days to request a hearing in writing, or schedule a hearing that can be moved one time.

Expect a final notice around January. From its postmark you have 30 days to take the matter to the Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board, which hears it from scratch and welcomes new evidence. Court comes after that, and the county advises talking to an attorney. Property missing from the roll can also be added by the Board, after the owner is notified.

Installment dates and late penalties

Bills go out in May. The first payment comes due 30 days after mailing. The second is due September 1, moving to the next working day if that is a weekend or Labor Day. Billing trails a year, meaning the payments you make this year cover the prior tax year. You get one bill with two tear-off coupons, never a second mailing.

Late payments cost 1 1/2% per month or fraction, even when only a day late. The Treasurer can give you the exact figure. A bill lost in the mail does not wipe out what you owe. Where a servicer pays from escrow, confirm with it so nothing is paid twice or missed.

Mobile homes run on their own calendar. Bills are mailed in April, the full tax is due within 60 days, and after that $25 a month or fraction accrues, up to $100. Selling or moving a mobile home requires a $10 tax certification.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Macon County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How a tax sale works

After second-installment posting is complete, a certified delinquent notice goes to the billing address, with $10 added for mailing and newspaper publication. The Treasurer also prints the owner's name, parcel number and amount due in a county paper. Unpaid tax then goes to the annual sale, where tax buyers bid interest downward starting at 9%, and the certificate goes to whoever bids lowest. What is bought is the tax, never the house.

On an owner-occupied home the redemption period is between 30 and 36 months, and you pay at the County Clerk's office. The payoff covers the tax sold, penalty, publication, sale costs, the buyer's other costs and the bid interest of up to 9%, compounded every six months. The statute generally gives 3 years from the sale but has exceptions (35 ILCS 200/21-350), so the Clerk can tell you which date applies to your certificate.

Exemptions and what changes at a sale

The smaller statutory homestead amounts apply here because no neighboring county has 3,000,000 or more people. A general homestead exemption can take as much as $6,000 off equalized assessed value (35 ILCS 200/15-175). Owners 65 or older living in the home may claim as much as $5,000 more (35 ILCS 200/15-170). The Supervisor of Assessments handles the paperwork.

Seniors can also ask the Treasurer about the Senior Citizens' Real Estate Tax Deferral Program. Affordable housing applications under 35 ILCS 200/10-260 go to the Supervisor, due September 1 of the assessment year.

When you sell, let the title company settle who owes which installment. The new owner should file a change of address form with the Treasurer by March 15, because the address on a recorded deed reaches that office late. If back taxes were sold, ask the Clerk for a redemption figure before accepting any offer. A cash buyer can close on that number.

Frequently asked questions

Where can I pay a Macon County tax bill?

Online at maconcountyil.us or at the Treasurer's counter, 141 South Main Street, Room 302, Decatur. For bill questions call 217-424-1426, and for payment site trouble call 844-400-8880.

What is the appeal deadline in Macon County?

Thirty calendar days after your township's publication date. No appeal is allowed afterward, so get the date from the Supervisor of Assessments.

Does Macon County send a second bill for the later installment?

No. One bill covers the year and carries two coupons. The second is due September 1, or the following working day when that date is a weekend or Labor Day.

Do I lose my Macon County house at the tax sale?

No. Buyers purchase only the unpaid tax, and you can still redeem by paying at the County Clerk's office.

What is the fee for mobile home tax certification in Macon County?

$10, by cash or check only. Bring the original title, have taxes paid to date, and give the Treasurer both the seller's and the buyer's names and addresses.

Offices that handle Macoupin County property tax

Three offices share the work: the Supervisor of Assessments, the Board of Review and the County Treasurer. The Supervisor is at 201 East Main in Carlinville (mail to P.O. Box 15, Carlinville, IL 62626) and answers at 217-854-8281. Staff there review the township assessors' work, equalize values across the county and publish assessment change notices.

Every year the Supervisor passes the assessment books to the Board of Review and prepares a tentative abstract for the Illinois Department of Revenue. The office also logs every property transaction, keeps parcel maps and exemption files, and holds the record of past owners. The Treasurer mails the bill and collects payment. Take what-do-I-owe questions to the Treasurer and what-is-my-house-worth questions to the assessment side.

Selling soon? Call both offices early. A title company will ask for your parcel number and the payoff on any unpaid installment before closing.

Macoupin County housing facts

Macoupin is a rural county of about 43,748 people (July 2025 estimate), and most homes are owner-occupied. Low turnover and few new builds mean older houses set the market, and assessors lean on recent sales of similar houses in the same township.

Macoupin County housing and income, 2020-2024
MeasureMacoupin County
Housing units21,263
Occupied homes with an owner living in them78.5%
Median owner-occupied home value$138,200
Median household income$70,805
Median gross rent$801 a month
Median owner costs with a mortgage$1,250 a month
Building permits, 202570

Farming, mainly corn and soybeans, remains the main industry. The county lies roughly midway between Springfield and St. Louis, so northern communities lean toward Springfield commuters and the southern end looks toward the Metro East. A sale in one corner can draw a different buyer pool than a sale in another.

How Macoupin County assesses a house

Outside Cook County the legal assessment is 33 1/3 percent of market value, with farmland and farm buildings treated separately. All property is reassessed every four years, and changes in other years are still published. Township assessors do the first-line work, then the Supervisor reviews and equalizes it.

To test your own number, divide the assessed value by the market value you would accept from a willing buyer, and compare the result with similar homes nearby. The county names four grounds for a reasonable complaint:

  • The assessor's market value is higher than the property would really sell for, which is easy to show if you bought recently or hold an appraisal.
  • Your assessment is a higher share of market value than the township or county median in a sales ratio study.
  • The record card has a wrong measurement, such as an incorrect lot or building size.
  • Similar neighboring properties carry lower assessments.

Mortgage holders must forward assessment change notices to borrowers within 15 days, so a notice may reach you through the lender as well as the mail.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Macoupin County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to appeal your assessment

Start with a written complaint to the Macoupin County Board of Review within 30 days after the township assessment roll is published. A mailed complaint counts if postmarked on or before the last day. Use the Board's form, sign as the owner, and file one form per parcel with your evidence attached.

The Board's published rules set the order of events:

  1. The Board gives every properly filed complaint a docket number and may inspect the property.
  2. It mails a proposed notice with a tentative decision, or it schedules a hearing.
  3. If you disagree with the tentative decision, you have 10 days from the proposed notice's postmark to ask for a hearing.
  4. The Board's clerk schedules hearings and mails you notice, then mails the final decision.

You may speak for yourself or hire an attorney. Useful evidence includes the transfer declaration, deed or purchase contract, an appraisal, recent comparable sales with photographs and record cards, and a copy of your own record card. If the result still looks wrong, you can appeal in writing to the Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board, or pay under protest and go to court. Courts are stricter and rarely favor an owner who skipped the administrative route.

The Board rules on the assessment, not on the tax bill. A complaint filed after the bill arrives is too late for that year.

What drives the size of your bill

Two inputs produce the bill: your assessment, and the amount your local taxing districts ask for. Assessment is a way to divide a fixed total among owners, so when a school or township raises its levy your bill moves even though your value did not.

Eight school districts serve the county: Bunker Hill CUSD 8, Carlinville CUSD 1, Gillespie CUSD 7, Mount Olive CUSD 5, North Mac CUSD 34, Northwestern CUSD 2, Southwestern CUSD 9 and Staunton CUSD 6. Your district is usually the biggest piece of the rate, so read the taxing bodies listed on your bill.

Selling with unpaid tax

Ask the Macoupin County Treasurer for installment dates and any balance, since the bill itself carries the due dates. Illinois counties sell unpaid taxes to tax buyers, so a title company will want a delinquent balance cleared before a deed is recorded. The Treasurer or the County Clerk can tell you what is owed on your parcel.

A lost bill is still owed, so ask the Treasurer for a duplicate. A sensible order for a seller: confirm what is paid, copy the parcel number from the bill, check that your homestead or senior exemption shows on it, and hand all of that to the title company. A cash buyer can work from the same paperwork and skip the lender's review.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Macoupin County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

A seller's tax checklist

Before you list, run through these steps in order:

  1. Pull the latest bill and note the parcel number and the taxing districts printed on it.
  2. Check that the homestead or senior exemption you qualify for appears on the bill. If it is missing, ask the Supervisor of Assessments how to apply.
  3. Look at your record card for wrong measurements, such as lot or building size. Correcting it before you list keeps the number buyers see accurate.
  4. Ask the Treasurer for the balance on any open installment, and ask the Treasurer or County Clerk whether older years were sold.
  5. Give the title company the parcel number, the bill and any payoff letters, so the year can be divided between you and the buyer at closing.

If a change notice arrives while the 30-day appeal window is open, decide quickly. A higher assessed value on your house also shows up on the buyer's first bill, and buyers do read it.

Frequently asked questions

When must I file a Macoupin County assessment complaint?

Within 30 days after your township's roll is published. A mailed complaint counts if postmarked on or before the last day. File one form per parcel and attach your evidence.

Can the Board of Review lower my tax bill?

No. It can only change the assessment. The bill follows from that and from the rates your taxing districts set, and once the bill is out the assessment for that year is closed.

What is the assessment level in Macoupin County?

33 1/3 percent of market value, except for farmland and farm buildings. All property is reassessed every four years, and changes in other years are published.

Which office answers assessment questions?

Call the Supervisor of Assessments at 217-854-8281, or write to P.O. Box 15, Carlinville, IL 62626. If you want to discuss your record card first, start with your township assessor.

What is the median home value in Macoupin County?

$138,200 for 2020-2024. Median household income over those years is $70,805, and owners live in 78.5 percent of occupied homes.

Billing and paying in Madison County

Property tax here goes through a Treasurer in Edwardsville, who bills in four installments. Due dates fall in July, September, October and December, on the 9th of each month, and bills go out in early June. Look for those months on your own bill.

The Treasurer's counter is in the Madison County Administration Building, 157 N. Main Street, Suite 125, Edwardsville, open weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Other ways to pay: online by e-check or card, by mailed check, or at one of nearly 100 collector banks and credit unions around the county, which require the bill coupon. Mail with the coupon goes to P.O. Box 849, and mail without it to P.O. Box 729, both in Edwardsville 62025. Cards add a 2.5 percent charge that goes to the card companies, and each transaction must be at least $2.50.

Partial online payments are not offered. To pay part of an installment, go to the office. Only an account holder can schedule all four installments in advance.

Late payment and the tax sale

Illinois law adds a 1.5 percent penalty every 30 days on the unpaid balance of a late installment. It starts one day after the deadline and runs until the installment is paid or the tax is sold. What follows:

  • A delinquency notice goes out by certified mail about a month before the annual tax sale, and a $10 certified fee is added to the bill.
  • Delinquent parcel numbers, owners and amounts are printed in a local newspaper.
  • Unpaid taxes are sold at the annual tax sale, and the owner can redeem for two to three years.
  • After the sale, the County Clerk mails a take notice for the tax buyer. Penalties bid at the sale run from 18 percent down to 0 percent, because bidding starts high and falls.
  • About two years after the sale, the Circuit Clerk and Sheriff tell the owner the buyer plans to ask the court for a tax deed. At about two and a half years, the buyer can petition for the deed.

Redemptions go through the Madison County Clerk and require the full amount owed, in cash, money order or cashier's check. Not receiving a bill is no defense, since 35 ILCS 200/20-15 says a failure to mail or receive a bill does not affect the tax. Call the Treasurer at (618) 692-6260 for a duplicate.

How Madison County sets assessments

Your township assessor, elected to a four-year term, inspects, lists and values each property, and the Chief County Assessment Office reviews those numbers. Assessed value is one-third of fair market value, so dividing the assessed value by .3333 shows the market value the office is using.

Before you file anything, the county suggests an informal talk with the assessor sometime from New Year's Day through the end of May in the assessment year.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Madison County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to appeal your assessment

If the informal talk does not settle it, file a formal complaint with the Board of Review, a three-member panel appointed by the County Board. The complaint session opens the day the Chief County Assessment Officer publishes assessment changes, and the window then stays open for 30 days. Only the Board's own forms are processed, with separate forms for residential, commercial and farm property, and an LLC must use an attorney. Mail forms to the Madison County Board of Review, 157 N. Main St., Suite 222, Edwardsville, IL 62025.

There are three grounds for an appeal:

  1. A fact on your property record card is wrong, such as the bath count or square footage.
  2. The estimated market value is too high, shown by recent sales or a purchase price below the assessed figure.
  3. The value may be accurate but is inequitable because similar homes are assessed lower.

The comparable grid asks for three similar properties. For an equity case, divide the improvement assessment by square footage for each home and compare. A complaint that taxes are too high will not win, because assessment officials set values, not taxes. Beyond the Board sits the five-member Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board.

After the bill arrives

Once the tax bill is out, it is too late to appeal that year's assessment. The assessment office finalizes values around the end of each year, certifies them to the state and passes them to the County Clerk, which closes the file. The one exception is a calculation error on the bill itself, such as an exemption that was never applied. Contact the assessment office if you spot one.

You can also pay under protest and file a tax objection complaint in circuit court, though a protest without a prior Board of Review appeal rarely goes well. Madison County is not covered by the Property Tax Extension Limitation Law that caps yearly increases in other counties.

About 220 taxing districts each adopt their own levy. Your bill multiplies the total rate per $100 of taxable assessed value by that value, then adds special assessments such as a drainage and levee district charge, which lands in the first installment.

Homestead exemptions

Several exemptions reduce the equalized assessed value before the rate is applied:

Madison County homestead exemptions
ExemptionReduction in EAV
General Homestead$6,000
Senior Homestead$5,000
Service-connected disability, 30 to 49 percent$2,500
Service-connected disability, 50 to 69 percent$5,000
Service-connected disability, 70 percent or moreExempt from taxation
Returning service members$5,000
Disabled Persons$2,000
Senior Citizen FreezeBased on freeze year and household income

You cannot freeze your taxes outright, but an owner 65 or older who lives in the home and has household income of $75,000 or less can apply for the Senior Citizens Assessment Freeze Homestead Exemption. Check your bill for these lines before you list a house. A missing exemption is a billing error you can fix.

The Madison County housing market

Madison is part of the Metro East beside St. Louis and the largest county in southern Illinois, with 263,110 residents (July 2025) and 119,947 housing units. Owner-occupancy is 74.2 percent, median owner-occupied value is $173,000, median household income is $75,793, and typical monthly rent is $1,024. Builders took out 435 permits in 2025. Edwardsville is the seat and Granite City is the largest city.

School districts include Edwardsville CUSD 7, Alton CUSD 11, Collinsville CUSD 10, Granite City CUSD 9 and Highland CUSD 5. Rates differ sharply by district, so compare the taxing bodies on your bill with those a buyer will see next door.

Selling with a Madison County tax bill

Installments come due in July, September, October and December, so a closing between dates can leave a partly paid year. Ask the Treasurer what is paid and what is open, and have the title company prorate the rest. If an older year went unpaid, get the County Clerk's redemption amount before you set a price. A cash buyer can close on those figures without waiting for a lender.

Frequently asked questions

When are Madison County property taxes due?

Four installments, due in July, September, October and December, on the 9th of each month. Mobile home tax is a separate single payment.

Does Madison County charge interest on late installments?

A 1.5 percent penalty applies to each late installment every 30 days after its due date. Unpaid taxes are eventually sold at the annual tax sale, and the owner can redeem for two to three years through the County Clerk.

What is the Madison County appeal deadline?

The Board of Review filing window stays open for 30 days from the day the Chief County Assessment Officer publishes assessment changes. After the tax bill comes out, that year's assessment can no longer be changed.

Who do I call with a question about my Madison County tax bill?

Call the Treasurer at (618) 692-6260 for payments and duplicate bills. For assessment or exemption problems, contact your township assessor or the Chief County Assessment Office.

Does Madison County cap how much taxes can rise?

No. The Property Tax Extension Limitation Law, which limits annual increases in other Illinois counties, does not apply here. Taxing districts set their own levies each year.

Marion County offices for tax questions

Two courthouse offices in Salem field most questions. The Supervisor of Assessments is at 100 E. Main St., Room 101, Salem, IL 62881, phone (618) 548-3853. The Treasurer is at 100 E. Main St., Suite 105, phone 618-548-3858.

The assessment office keeps a property record card for every parcel, listing the characteristics being assessed. It also updates ownership after a deed is recorded with the Marion County Recorder. A change of mailing address must be made in writing, either on the county's form or in person. If you sell, send the new owner's tax bill address to this office as soon as the deed is recorded, so the next bill reaches the right person.

The assessment office values property and has no control over how much tax you pay. The taxing bodies on your bill decide what they need, and that sets the dollar amount.

Ways to pay in Marion County

You can pay at a local bank, by mail, on the web, in a courthouse drop box or at the counter in Salem. Authorized banks include First Financial Bank, Farmer's State Bank, US Bank, Iuka State Bank, Kaskaskia Valley Credit Union, Kinmundy Bank, Marion County Saving Bank, FNB Patoka, People's National Bank, Midland States Bank, Gen Fed Credit Union and Peoples State Bank. A bank needs the payment stub and will not take anything after the second installment due date.

  • Mail checks to Marion County Treasurer, 100 East Main, Room 105, P.O. Box 1025, Salem, IL 62881, payable to Marion County Collector.
  • Enclose the stub from the bottom of the bill. If you lost the bill, add $2.00 for homeowners or $5.00 for mortgage companies and banks to reprint it.
  • Put the parcel number on the check, date it today, and write it for the full installment. Partial payments and post-dated checks are refused.
  • A letter postmarked by the due date counts as paid on time.
  • The secure drop box is at the courthouse's west entrance and is checked daily. Anything dropped off after 4:30 in the afternoon posts the next business day.

Online, cards go through the county's payment portal with a 2.25 percent fee plus $1.50 per transaction, and an e-check is a flat $2.00. None of that goes to the county. Personal checks are good until 30 days before the tax sale. After that the Treasurer wants certified funds: cash, a cashier's check or a money order.

Homestead and other exemptions

Each exemption ties to a section of the Property Tax Code. Check that yours appears on your bill, because the General Homestead must be listed for a principal residence.

Marion County homestead exemptions
ExemptionStatuteAmount or condition
General Homestead35 ILCS 200/15-175Up to $6,000 off assessed valuation
Senior Citizen Homestead35 ILCS 200/15-170$5,000 reduction; owner reaches 65 before year end of the taxing year

Owners with a service-connected disability have two more routes. A specially adapted house can be exempt up to $100,000 of assessed value, with certification from the state. The standard exemption is $2,500 at a 30 to 49 percent rating, $5,000 at 50 to 69 percent, and full exemption at 70 percent or more, provided total EAV stays under $250,000. These owners must file yearly by July 1.

The Homestead Improvement exemption is capped at $25,000 of assessed value, or $75,000 of fair cash value, per year. A Natural Disaster exemption covers a rebuilt principal residence, as long as it is no larger than 110 percent of the original and is rebuilt within two years.

If your Marion County assessment looks too high

Start by talking with the assessment office, where staff will explain how the value was reached and which exemptions apply. Ask yourself the office's own test: would you sell for the market value on the bill, or higher? If not, gather evidence. The Board of Review is the formal route, and the filing dates are printed on your change of assessment notice. Keep the notice and ask the Supervisor's office to confirm the deadline for your township.

Before filing, get your property record card. A wrong square footage, bath count or year built is the easiest error to prove. A recent sale, a closing statement or an appraisal backs up a value claim, while photos and assessments of nearby similar homes back up a uniformity claim. If the county board's answer disappoints you, the state's Property Tax Appeal Board hears the next round.

Marion County has seventeen townships, and the county website lists the township assessors. A township assessor can often fix a data error faster than a formal appeal can.

Marion County housing market

Marion is a smaller, lower-value market. About 36,382 people lived here in July 2025, a 3.6 percent decline since 2020. There are 17,396 housing units, and owners live in 74.7 percent of occupied homes. A typical owned home is valued at $103,000 for 2020-2024, median household income is $61,240, and rent is about $794 a month. Only 12 building permits were issued in 2025.

With so little new construction, the existing housing stock sets prices. A buyer will compare your house with other older homes, so condition matters more than new-build competition. Salem holds the courthouse and Centralia is the biggest city, and the four incorporated cities are Centralia, Kinmundy, Salem and Wamac.

Selling with taxes in mind

Ask the Treasurer for the amount due on any open installment before you list, and ask which installments are already paid. Because the bank, the title company and the Treasurer all need the same parcel number, copy it from the bill into your sale file. Partial payments are not accepted, so any payoff has to cover the full installment plus penalty or interest if you are late.

Confirm that the General Homestead shows on your bill. Then send the buyer's bill address to the assessment office once the deed is recorded. A cash buyer can close on the Treasurer's payoff figure without waiting on a lender's tax review.

Hand the title company your latest bill, the payment receipts for any installment you have already paid, and the name and address the buyer wants on the next bill. Having these ready keeps the closing statement clean and avoids a second trip to the courthouse.

Where do I pay Marion County property taxes in person?

At the Treasurer's office in the Marion County Courthouse, 100 East Main Street, Salem, on weekdays. A secure drop box sits at the courthouse's west entrance. Bring the payment stub from your bill.

Can I make a partial payment in Marion County?

No. A check has to cover the full installment, including any penalty or interest if you are late.

What is the Marion County online payment fee?

Cards carry a 2.25 percent fee plus $1.50 per transaction, and an e-check costs a flat $2.00. The fees go to the payment processor, not to the county.

Which exemption applies to the home I live in?

The General Homestead Exemption, up to $6,000 of assessed valuation, applies to an owner-occupied principal residence. Seniors, service members and disabled owners may qualify for more, so confirm each with the Supervisor of Assessments.

How much is a typical Marion County home worth?

Montgomery County housing market

Montgomery County is in south-central Illinois. Hillsboro is the seat and Litchfield is the biggest city. Population slid from 30,104 in 2010 to 28,288 in 2020, with a July 2025 estimate of 28,076. Values are modest, yet a seller still has to clear every open tax installment before closing.

Montgomery County housing and income

Housing units, July 1, 202512,528
Owner-occupied rate, 2020-202477.4%
Median value, owned homes$112,300
