Winters near Hillsboro bring January lows around 21 degrees and summers push July highs to about 91, so roofs and foundations go through freeze and bake cycles. Buyers' inspectors tend to look hard at both.

Which office answers which tax question

Four desks split the work:

  • Treasurer and ex-officio collector: mails and collects real estate, drainage and mobile home tax and runs the yearly sale. Room 101, 1 Courthouse Square, Hillsboro, phone (217) 532-9521.
  • County Clerk and Recorder: works out each parcel's rate, handles redemption of sold taxes and records deeds. Call (217) 532-9530 about rates and redemption, and (217) 532-9535 about recording.
  • Supervisor of Assessments: runs the assessment cycle, processes exemptions and looks up parcel numbers. Room 201, (217) 532-9595.
  • Board of Review: hears value complaints, in the Supervisor's suite.

Value questions start with the township assessor, and bill questions with the Treasurer. Calling the right desk first saves a transfer.

Paying a Montgomery County bill

The Treasurer takes payment five ways:

  • Mail, addressed to the Treasurer at 1 Courthouse Square, Room 101, Hillsboro, IL 62049.
  • In person at Room 101 of the Historic Courthouse.
  • A gray metal drop box by the fire escape on the courthouse's north face.
  • The automated line, (217) 627-6183.
  • The online link on the Treasurer's web page.

Under Public Act 104-0553, the county now buys its own delinquent real estate taxes as trustee for the districts, starting with the sale for tax year 2025. Delinquent mobile home taxes still go to private bidders.

If you like to pay early, ask about the prepayment contract. Your deposit sits in trust against the coming bill, any shortfall is due by the second due date, extra money is refunded, and the interest stays with the county.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Montgomery County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Due dates and late interest

Each year's bill prints its own dates, so read the stubs. By state law the first installment is delinquent after the later of June 1 and the day following its printed date, and the second after the later of September 1 and the day following its printed date (35 ILCS 200/21-15). Interest is 1 1/2% for each month or fraction.

Mail postmarked by the deadline is on time. Tax is owed even if no bill arrives, so a new owner who never got one should phone the Treasurer for the amount and ask who is listed as taxpayer of record.

The name printed on a bill is there for mailing only. Ownership is shown by the last deed on file with the Recorder.

How a home's value becomes a tax figure

Township assessors set values, and equalization factors from the Supervisor's office bring the level to 33 1/3 percent of market. Subtract exemptions and you have the base the levies apply to. Each district certifies what it needs, the Clerk converts that to a rate, and the rate times equalized value is your tax.

A district may raise its levy up to 5 percent over what it collected the prior year. Anything higher forces a Truth-in-Taxation hearing, which is informational and needs no vote. If your bill climbs, one of three things is behind it: a higher rate, a higher assessment, or an exemption you are missing.

Special areas add wrinkles. A parcel in a TIF district owes the same total, but part flows to the TIF fund. Drainage charges are set by the district with court approval, and an annexed parcel takes on the new district's rate.

How to appeal your assessment

Talk to the township assessor first, then the Supervisor at (217) 532-9595, and go formal only if the answers do not satisfy you. The Board of Review meets from the first Monday of June, with extra sessions as the workload requires. State law gives you 30 calendar days after the assessment list is published (35 ILCS 200/16-55).

There is a second route for the current year's tax: an objection filed with the Circuit Clerk, (217) 532-9546. Protests aimed at future years go to the Board through the Supervisor. The paths differ, so ask which one fits before paying any fee.

Either way the dispute is about value, not the dollar tax. The Supervisor also invites neighbors to report a property that looks under-assessed, since errors in either direction shift the rate for everyone.

If a bill goes unpaid

Whatever stays unpaid goes to the Treasurer's annual sale. Afterward you can still redeem for two to three years, depending on property type, though interest and fees make it costlier.

  • The Clerk issues an Estimate of Redemption. Check that it names the right parcel.
  • Pay in cash, certified funds or a money order to the Montgomery County Clerk. No payment plans exist.
  • If you miss the next year's second installment, the buyer may purchase that year too, at 12%.
  • Tax deed process costs are added to the redemption figure.

After a sale the Clerk's office mails a Take Notice, and the delinquent list runs in local papers beforehand. Keep a copy of every check or receipt, since that is your best defense if a payment is not credited.

Exemptions for homeowners

The general homestead exemption covers an owner's principal residence and is capped at a $6,000 reduction in equalized value for a county like this one (35 ILCS 200/15-175). The Supervisor's office also helps applicants complete the Senior Homestead Exemption and Senior Citizens Assessment Freeze forms.

The freeze form is refiled each year, since household income shifts when someone moves in or out. Ask the Supervisor's office which forms you need after a move.

Closing checklist for sellers

Gather the parcel number, request current and prior bills from the Treasurer, and ask the Clerk if any year was sold. The title company prorates the current year, and the settlement statement shows what is paid or owed.

The deed also has to pass the Recorder's checklist: street address and parcel number beside the legal description, a notarized Plat Act Affidavit, and a "future taxes to" name and address. Margins are specific, with a two inch gap at the upper right of page one and one inch on later pages. The description printed on a tax bill is not a full legal description and will be refused.

The Recorder offers a free Property Fraud Alert sign-up that notifies you by email or phone whenever a document is recorded under your name. It is a sensible safeguard around a sale. A cash sale skips the lender's review but not the Recorder's checklist.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Who answers Treasurer questions in Montgomery County?

The Treasurer's office, at (217) 532-9521 in Room 101 of the Historic Courthouse, also supplies copies of current or past bills. Card and phone payments run through (217) 627-6183.

Is there a payment plan to redeem sold Montgomery County taxes?

No. The County Clerk takes only cash, certified funds or a money order and offers no installments. Request an Estimate of Redemption at (217) 532-9530 before sending money.

Who calculates the rate on my bill?

The County Clerk. Each taxing body certifies a levy, the Clerk's staff divides it by the valuation within statutory limits, and the Treasurer prints and mails the result.

Is the name on my bill proof of ownership?

No. The bill's name and address are for mailing only, and the last recorded deed identifies the owner.

Where does an assessment complaint go?

To the Board of Review through the Supervisor of Assessments, (217) 532-9595, within 30 calendar days of the list's publication.

Billing and valuation sit in different offices. The Treasurer, at 300 West State Street in Jacksonville, mails bills and takes payment. The Supervisor of Assessments values every parcel and processes exemptions. The three County Commissioners hear complaints as the Board of Review, with the Supervisor acting as clerk.

Two more players appear on your bill that the county does not control: the township assessor, who does the first valuation, and the taxing districts, whose levies set the rate. The county's pages also list three tax increment financing districts, two in Jacksonville and one in Meredosia, and one enterprise zone in Jacksonville. Contact the city or village hall for details on those.

The yearly Morgan County payment calendar

Bills for each tax year are mailed in the spring and paid the following year, and the Treasurer's page posts the exact dates each year. The usual sequence:

Typical Morgan County Treasurer schedule

Penalties on the first installment start the day after the due date at 1.5% and rise 1.5 points each month, reaching 7.5% in October. The second installment starts at 1.5% and steps to 3% a month later. Mobile home penalties begin at $25 and grow by $25 a month up to $100. A $10 certified mailing fee is added to accounts that receive a certified letter. Reminders go out in September, certified letters in early October, and would-be tax buyers must register ahead of the sale with a $100 refundable fee.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Morgan County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to pay

You can pay by mail, in the drop box, at any Morgan County bank other than US Bank, or through an online portal. Mail goes to Morgan County Treasurer, 300 West State Street, Jacksonville, IL 62650. The drop box is outside the courthouse's north entrance and is emptied each day.

  • Include the detachable stub from the bill with every payment.
  • Make checks payable to Morgan County Treasurer. A cancelled check is your receipt.
  • Returned checks carry a $25 charge, and post-dated checks are illegal and will not be held.
  • Only one bill comes each year, so keep the second stub. A duplicate bill costs $2.
  • Not getting a bill, or getting it late, never cancels the tax or penalty.

If the bill is not yours to pay, pass it to the owner or send it back to the Treasurer.

How the Supervisor values a house

Homes are valued at 33.33% of market value, with farmland and farm buildings treated separately. The office starts from square footage and story height, adds or subtracts for features such as bathrooms, central air, fireplaces, decks and garages, and then applies depreciation for age and condition. The base price assumes a full basement, central heat, one bath and a kitchen sink.

Land is valued as if vacant, by front foot, square foot, acreage or a flat site value for a whole area. The county and state then equalize values using three previous years of sales, which keeps one hot year from whipsawing assessments. Farm buildings are valued by use as well as size, so a newer pole building that sits idle can carry almost no contributory value. Mobile homes on piers are generally taxed through a privilege tax, while those on a permanent foundation are assessed as real estate and can claim the same exemptions as a frame or brick house.

How to appeal your assessment

You have 30 days from publication of the assessment list, which usually runs in late December. File with the Supervisor by day 30, stating your reason and attaching proof: a recent sale, comparables, an appraisal or neighboring assessments (35 ILCS 200/16-55).

Next, the Board mails a proposed change notice showing the old value and any adjustment. If you disagree, you can ask for a formal hearing. When hearings end, final changes go out and the books close. An owner still unhappy can take the case to the state Property Tax Appeal Board within 30 days of receiving the final notice, using forms kept at the assessor's office.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Morgan County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Homestead exemption

Exemptions go to people who own the home, live in it as a principal residence and are responsible for the tax. Rentals and commercial or industrial property are excluded. For the general homestead exemption, a county that does not border one of 3 million people, as Morgan does not, has a $6,000 cap on the equalized value reduction (35 ILCS 200/15-175).

Ask the Supervisor's office which other exemptions fit your situation and when to file.

Before closing: taxes and the Treasurer

Start at the Treasurer's counter and ask what each installment owes, plus any older delinquent year. A mailed payment is timely if postmarked by the due date, and first-installment delinquency begins at the later of June 1 or the day after the date on the bill (35 ILCS 200/21-15).

The title company splits the year between you and the buyer at closing. If a lender escrows the tax, ask the servicer what it has already sent so nothing gets paid twice. Because the tax sale is the cutoff on the Treasurer's calendar, clear any unpaid balance before the October dates. A cash buyer can close on the Treasurer's payoff figure and skip a lender's review.

What to bring to the Treasurer and the title company

Collect your latest bill with both stubs, any cancelled checks that prove earlier payments, and the parcel number. If you have lost the bill, a duplicate is $2. Check that your homestead exemption appears on it, and ask the Supervisor's office about any exemption you think is missing.

If the house sits in a TIF district or the enterprise zone, tell the title company and the buyer, and send them to the city or village hall for the rules. For a mobile home, say whether it sits on piers or a permanent foundation, since that decides whether it is taxed as real estate. Giving your closer these facts early lets them prepare a settlement statement without surprises.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

When do second installment penalties start in Morgan County?

The day after the due date, mid September, at 1.5%, rising to 3% a month later. The first installment is due in late June, with penalties starting the next day.

Can a Morgan County bill be paid at a bank?

Yes, at any Morgan County bank except US Bank. Mail, the drop box outside the courthouse's north entrance and the online portal also work.

What does a replacement bill cost?

$2.00 for a duplicate. One bill carries both installments each year, so keep it. A bill that never reached you does not remove the tax.

Who decides assessment complaints in Morgan County?

The three County Commissioners sit as the Board of Review, with the Supervisor of Assessments as clerk. Appeals are accepted for 30 days after the list is published.

Are there TIF districts in Morgan County?

Yes, three: two in Jacksonville and one in Meredosia, along with a single enterprise zone in Jacksonville. The local city or village hall has the rules for each.

Cash Home Buyers in Illinois

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Ogle County at a glance

Ogle County spreads across northern Illinois below Rockford. Oregon holds the courthouse, while Rochelle is the county's most populous city. Freight rail runs through it, and farming, chiefly corn and soybeans, sits beside manufacturing as a major activity. The county had 51,399 residents in mid-2025, down from 51,788 in 2020 and 53,497 in 2010.

Ogle County housing figures
MeasureValue
Homes and apartments, mid-202522,783
Share lived in by owners75.4%
Middle value, owned homes$189,200
Middle gross rent$936
Middle household income$82,132
Permits issued in 202587

Owners with a mortgage report median monthly costs of $1,533, and owners without one $672. Winters here get cold, with a record low of minus 27 at Oregon, so buyers will look closely at insulation and heating.

What the Treasurer handles

Collection of real estate and mobile home tax belongs to the Treasurer, who then distributes it to each taxing body. Visit the old Courthouse, 105 S. 5th Street, Oregon, weekdays between 8:30 and 4:30, closed on holidays. By mail, use Ogle County Collector, P.O. Box 40, Oregon, IL 61061.

Valuation sits with the Supervisor of Assessments at (815) 732-1150. Roughly 60 percent of a bill funds the local school district, with the rest shared by the county, municipalities, parks, libraries, fire districts, townships and special districts. Springfield writes the rules yet takes none of the money.

Due dates and penalties

Bills for 2025 were mailed May 1, 2026, and one document carries stubs for both installments. The Treasurer cautions that nothing else arrives ahead of the second, so keep it. The calendar repeats each year with new days.

  • Mobile home tax: mid-May.
  • First installment: early June.
  • Second installment: early September.
  • Certified funds only, with no online payments: about a month before the last day to pay.
  • Last day to pay: early November.
  • Tax sale of real estate and mobile homes: the day after the last day to pay.

The county charges 1.5% for every month a payment runs late, and a partial month is billed as a whole one. Mail postmarked by the due date stays on time under state law, which marks first-installment delinquency at the later of June 1 or the day following the printed date (35 ILCS 200/21-15).

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Ogle County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to pay or search a bill

Accepted forms are cash, a check payable to Ogle County Collector, or a credit card, either at the Treasurer's desk or at any bank in Ogle County. An online option exists too. It adds a fee you should review first, and it gives a confirmation worth keeping.

The county's lookup works from an address or a 10-digit parcel number. Enter just the house number and street name, skipping N or S and endings like Ave. The public cannot see owner names. A prepayment program takes deposits between December 1 and April 1 using a form from the Treasurer's website.

The Treasurer's page also links an undeliverable tax bill listing, worth checking if a bill may have gone to an old address. Ahead of a sale, run the parcel in the lookup and ask the office whether any earlier year is still open.

How Ogle County assesses a home

Farmland aside, the target is one third of market value, applied evenly across a jurisdiction. An elected township assessor places the first values on property inside the township, and the Supervisor of Assessments oversees that work for the county.

Ogle County has 24 townships, among them Oregon-Nashua, Byron, Mount Morris, Flagg, Pine Rock and Scott, and the appeal deadline is tied to the publication for your township. Call the Supervisor's office first for a parcel you have not owned before. Local officials are also the ones to ask about a surprising bill, since the tax stays in the community that pays it.

How to appeal your assessment

A three-person Board of Review, appointed by the County Board under 35 ILCS 200/16-20, takes the case. Its seats split two to one between the parties. The filing window is generally 30 days after your township's assessment list appears, matching the current-year rule in 35 ILCS 200/16-55.

  • Send by U.S. Mail with a postmark on or before the last day, or hand it in by then.
  • Faxes, emails and other electronic filings are refused.
  • Read the Board's rules and the form's instructions beforehand. Commercial property has its own form, and a Request to Intervene form is available.

The Board weighs what the owner and the township assessor submit and may set a hearing. Meetings pick up in November, December and January once deadlines pass, and the same Board decides exemption requests.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Ogle County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Homestead relief

State law caps the general homestead reduction at $6,000 of equalized value for counties such as Ogle that do not touch a 3,000,000-resident county (35 ILCS 200/15-175). Requests for other exemptions go to the Board of Review.

Illinois also has senior and veteran programs. Call the Supervisor of Assessments at (815) 732-1150 to learn which applications fit your household.

Before you list an Ogle County house

Start with the lookup. Search by address or the 10-digit parcel number, note which installments show as paid, and compare that with what your lender escrowed. If a bill may have gone to an old address, check the undeliverable bill listing on the Treasurer's page.

Next, call the Treasurer at the Courthouse in Oregon for a written payoff on any open installment, and call the Supervisor of Assessments if the assessed value looks off. If your township's assessment list was published recently, the 30 day appeal window may still be open, so ask before you set a price. Give the payoff and exemption details to the title company early, so the settlement statement matches the county's records on closing day.

Settling taxes when you sell

Pull the parcel in the online lookup, then ask the Treasurer for the payoff on whatever installment is open. At closing the title company prorates the year, and the settlement statement lists each side's share.

Balances still unpaid after the final payment day go to the tax sale. Following a sale, the owner of a one-to-six unit residence has at least 2 1/2 years to redeem, other property at least 2 years, and a tax buyer may stretch either to 3 years (35 ILCS 200/21-350).

A cash buyer can close without waiting on a lender, but the title work is the same: the unpaid balance is cleared from your proceeds, and the deed does not record until the tax office confirms the figure.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

When is the last day to pay Ogle County taxes before the sale?

It falls in early November, one day ahead of the tax sale. About a month earlier only certified funds are taken and online payments end.

Does Ogle County mail a separate second installment bill?

No. One bill with two stubs is mailed, and the Treasurer says nothing more comes before the second installment, so keep it.

How do I find my Ogle County parcel number?

Look on the tax bill for a 10-digit number, usually formatted XX-XX-XXX-XXX. The online lookup can also find it from a house number and street name.

Can I file an Ogle County assessment appeal by email?

No. The Board takes appeals only by postmarked U.S. Mail or hand delivery by the deadline, and it does not accept fax or electronic filings.

Who owes the late fee on an Ogle County bill?

The property owner does. The fee is 1.5% per month, a fraction of a month counts as a full one, and a mailed payment avoids it only when postmarked by the due date.

Selling in Peoria County? Get a Cash Offer

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Peoria County?
We buy Peoria County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Four offices, one bill

Peoria County splits the tax job among four courthouse offices. One official acts as both Treasurer and County Collector, so the bill and the payment counter are in the same place. Valuation sits with the Supervisor of Assessments, disputes go to the Board of Review, and the County Clerk turns levies into rates and later receives money for any year that was sold. Your first call about value belongs with the township assessor.

Peoria and West Peoria are treated as independent of the surrounding townships, so a house in either place deals with a city township office while a rural parcel deals with its own township.

  • Treasurer: mails and collects the bills from 324 Main Street, Room G15.
  • Supervisor of Assessments: publishes assessment changes and handles exemption questions at 309-672-6910.
  • Board of Review: three people named by the County Board, working from Room 301.
  • County Clerk: extends the tax rate and receives payment of sold taxes at Room 101.

Housing in the county

The county has an estimated 178,553 residents, which is 1.9% below the 2020 base, and 84,884 housing units. Of 77,755 households, 67.0% own their home, and the median owned home is worth $158,500. Median rent is $993 and median household income is $65,108. Those are modest price points, so a tax bill that runs high for the neighborhood can weigh on a sale.

How bills are issued and what a late payment costs

Each parcel gets a single annual bill that can be paid in two equal halves. For 2025 taxes, payable in 2026, bills were scheduled to go out by May 1, with installments due in June and September. If nothing has arrived by May 15, call 672-6065 and choose option 5. Not receiving a bill is no excuse for skipping the payment.

Money that arrives or is postmarked after the due date picks up 1.5% for each month or part of one. Metered postage does not prove timeliness, and the Treasurer adds that the Peoria postal facility has stopped stamping postmarks, so mail early or use another channel.

  • Counter and mail payments can be cash (in the office only), personal check, cashier's check or money order.
  • Online and phone payments open after May 1. Cards, Apple Pay, Google Pay, PayPal and Venmo carry a 2.65% convenience fee, and an electronic check costs $1.00.
  • Phone payments add $0.95 per parcel, and none of the processing fees go to the county.
  • A check returned by the bank costs $25.00.
  • A short payment is returned and the installment stays open, so cover the whole amount plus any penalty.
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Peoria County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

The yearly tax calendar

The order of events repeats every year with new days. This is the pattern for 2025 taxes payable in 2026.

Peoria County yearly cycle
StepTiming
Tax bills mailedBy May 1
First installmentEarly June
Second installmentEarly September
Board of Review filing deadlineLate September
Final notices of unpaid tax mailedBy mid-October
Last day to pay at the Treasurer to avoid the saleEarly November, 5 p.m.
Annual tax saleThe next business day or so after

The collector charges $10 once final notices are sent, covering registered mail and the published list, and $113 more is added at the sale itself. Have the Treasurer put the precise payoff in writing before money moves.

How to appeal your assessment

Values are set as of January 1. The 2026 taxpayer notice sets the required level at 33.33% of fair market value, while the county's median level came in at 31.25%. An equalization factor is applied by township and class, exemptions come off, and the rate is multiplied against what remains.

The county strongly suggests an informal talk with the township assessor first. A formal Board of Review complaint can follow any time from June 1 up to 30 days after the newspaper prints your township's changes. This year's window closed September 30, so the next one opens June 1.

  • The form challenges value, not the size of the bill, and any change shows up on next year's bill rather than the one in hand.
  • Attach your evidence when you file. The Board can raise the value, lower it or confirm it.
  • A missed hearing is decided on the paperwork alone, and dates cannot be moved.
  • Packets are posted under Forms and Documents. Mail filings to Room 301 of the courthouse.

Exemptions and tax relief

Nearly all of these cut the equalized assessed value, so the dollar effect depends on your district's rate.

  • Owner-occupied (homestead): $6,000 off equalized assessed value for residents as of January 1. The township assessor initiates it, with no annual application.
  • Senior homestead: another $5,000 once you turn 65 in the tax year. File at the Assessor's Office with a deed copy and proof of age, one time only.
  • Senior assessment freeze: locks the taxable value for seniors under an income ceiling of $65,000, with a new application each year. Confirm the ceiling for your filing year with the Supervisor of Assessments.
  • Returning service members: a one-time $5,000 reduction.
  • Disabled persons: $2,000 reduction, renewed each year.
  • Disabled service members: $2,500 for a 30% to under 50% service-connected rating, $5,000 for 50% to under 70%, and a fully exempt residence at 70% or higher.
  • Senior tax deferral: a 3% interest loan against the home, repaid at sale or death, with a March 1 filing deadline.
Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Peoria County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with unpaid taxes

Delinquent tax goes to a sale in early November. Registered buyers bid between 0% and 9% and the lowest number takes the lien. A parcel with no bidder is taken by Peoria County, as trustee for the districts, at 9%. That interest is charged at the sale and again every six months.

You remain the owner while the redemption clock runs, since what gets sold is the tax debt. Two years is the default and a buyer may push it to three, with two and a half years as the floor for residences of one to six units. A judge reviews the buyer's request for a deed once time runs out.

To redeem, go to the County Clerk at 324 Main Street, Room 101, with a single payment of cash, a cashier's check or a money order made out to the Peoria County Clerk. Personal, business, mortgage and title company checks bounce back, and installment plans do not exist. Call (309) 672-6060. An online redemption estimate shows when the next penalty lands.

Handling taxes at closing

Request a payoff from the Treasurer for the current year and one from the Clerk if any year was sold, and hand both to the title company. Sold taxes are cleared by redemption at the Clerk's office, and because the payoff grows every six months, the number you use needs a date near closing.

At propertytax.peoriacounty.gov you can look up a parcel, its bill history and a printable bill. If the house is in the city of Peoria, find out whether you pay the City of Peoria Township Collector, because the county sets that office apart from its own counter. When a lender escrows the tax, confirm that the latest installment was credited to the right parcel number.

Frequently asked questions

Where can Peoria County tax be paid at a counter?

At the Treasurer's office, 324 Main Street, Room G15, at a participating bank, or at a township collector. A bank needs the bill stub with the payment. The City of Peoria Township Collector serves its own residents.

When does a Peoria County complaint have to be filed?

The window opens June 1 and closes 30 days after the newspaper publishes your township's changes. Call the Board of Review at 309-672-6022 for the current schedule.

Can I pay only part of an installment in Peoria County?

No. A partial payment is mailed back and the installment remains unpaid until the full amount, penalty included, comes in. Electronic payments that do not match the exact figure are rejected.

Does an owner-occupied exemption need a yearly application in Peoria County?

No. The township assessor sets up the $6,000 owner-occupied exemption without a yearly form. Seniors file the homestead exemption once, but the assessment freeze and the disabled persons exemption need renewing each year.

What is the redemption period after a Peoria County tax sale?

Two years is the default and the buyer can extend to three. For one-to-six unit homes the floor is two and a half years. Pay the County Clerk once, in full, with cash, a cashier's check or a money order.

Rock Island County, IL Property Tax Guide: Offices, Appeals and Selling With Tax Due

Cash Home Buyers in Illinois
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Rock Island County, IL Property Tax Guide: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Rock Island County, IL Property Tax Guide sale

Selling in Rock Island County? Get a Cash Offer

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Rock Island County?
We buy Rock Island County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Offices that touch your bill

Rock Island County borders the Mississippi on Illinois's western edge. The seat is the city of Rock Island, and Moline, next door, is the biggest city. Five offices share the tax work.

  • County Treasurer and Collector: mails the bills and receives payments at 1504 3rd Avenue, Rock Island, IL 61201.
  • Chief County Assessment Office: upstairs in that building, 309-558-3660. Staff are there weekdays through 4:30 p.m.
  • Township assessors: where questions about value start, across the county's 18 townships.
  • Board of Review: three people chosen by the County Board who rule on appeals.
  • County Clerk, Delinquent Tax Division: takes redemption payments, 309-558-3562.

Housing in the county

The county has an estimated 141,869 people, a 1.9% decline since 2020, living among 66,873 housing units. Owners occupy 69.7% of homes. Half of owner-occupied homes were worth more than $150,400, rent runs $889 at the median and households typically take in $67,159. The commute averages 19.7 minutes, and Interstates 74, 80, 88 and 280 all run through the county.

Due dates: four installments

The yearly bill is cut into four payments here. They go in order, each in full, with penalty interest added where it applies. Bills for 2025 taxes were due out on or before May 1, 2026.

Rock Island County installments
InstallmentUsual due date
FirstAround June 10
SecondAround August 10
ThirdAround September 10
FourthAround November 10

The pattern repeats each year, and the Treasurer posts the exact days once bills are out.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Rock Island County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to pay

Six channels exist, each with its own cutoff, and a few close before the last due date.

  • Bank or credit union: at participating branches until the final due date. Bring the whole bill with stubs, and no cards.
  • Mail: address it to the Rock Island County Collector, PO Box 3277, Rock Island, IL 61204-3277, with a postmark no later than the due date.
  • In person: at the County Office Building. Cash, check, cashier's check and money order are taken, and cards and mobile wallets work until a few days after the final due date.
  • Drop box: in the alley and parking lot behind the County Office Building.
  • Online and phone: by e-check, card or wallet, with the phone line at 309-518-9200.
  • Autopay: online enrollment is offered.

The card processor, not the county, keeps the processing fees: $1.00 for an e-check, and 2.45% for cards and wallets or $2.00 when the transaction is under $82.00. Other charges are $30 for a returned payment and $2 for a duplicate bill. A mortgage company that wants a memo bill instead of stubs pays $5 per parcel.

How to contest an assessment

Township assessors set values as of January 1. The county assessment officer reviews and equalizes them, and the Board of Review takes complaints. If the result still seems wrong, the next stop is the State Property Tax Appeal Board, a five-member panel.

Complaining that taxes are high will not win. There are three grounds: errors on the property record card, a market value above what similar homes sold for, or a fair value that still exceeds comparable properties. Useful evidence includes a recent appraisal, nearby sales, photographs of condition or a chart of comparable assessments.

The window is 30 days from newspaper publication, and once assessments are certified to the state the files are closed. Ask the township assessor when the next window opens. Routine upkeep rarely raises an assessment, though a deck, porch, in-ground pool or fireplace can.

What to do before closing

Pull the parcel in the county's online lookup and print the current and prior-year bills. Ask the Treasurer which installments are paid, and note that installments are taken in order, so an unpaid early one blocks the later ones. If a mortgage company escrows the tax, get the servicer's payment history.

Call the Delinquent Tax Division at 309-558-3562 if there is any chance a year went to sale, because redemption must be paid in one lump and the figure changes with the date. Give the title company the payoff in writing. Sellers who plan a cash sale still need clear tax records, since a buyer's attorney will ask for them, but there is no lender review to wait on. Keep copies of every receipt, because a mismatch between the lender's records and the county's is the usual cause of a surprise at the table.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Rock Island County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Exemptions and the senior freeze

The county's Property Tax Relief page lists the programs, and the assessment office fields questions on each.

  • Owner-occupied: takes up to $6,000 off equalized assessed value if you lived in the home by the January 1 that begins the assessment year. File with the township assessor or at the county office.
  • Senior freeze: holds the taxable assessment steady while the rate keeps moving. Applicants need two straight Januarys of owning and living in the home, a 65th birthday within the assessment year, the senior homestead exemption and household income under the cap. Applications are due July 1 and renew each year.
  • Others: disabled persons, disabled and returning service members, natural disaster, and several charitable forms.

A state law signed in December 2025 lifts the senior freeze income cap. The limit is $65,000 for tax year 2025, $75,000 for 2026, $77,000 for 2027 and $79,000 for 2028, and it stays at $79,000 after that unless the General Assembly acts.

Selling with taxes owed

Any installment still open after the fourth due date rolls into the annual tax sale. A certified-mail notice and newspaper listing follow within weeks, carrying a $10 fee. At the sale the county adds $94 in miscellaneous fees and $160 for canceling the sale and issuing certificates of redemption, and interest can range from 18% down to 0% depending on the winning bid.

Ownership does not move at the sale. The owner can redeem for two and a half to three years, with the buyer choosing the length. The County Clerk accepts cash, a cashier's check, a certified check or a money order, all in one lump. Call the Delinquent Tax Division, 309-558-3562, for a figure before you schedule a closing.

Escrow can hide problems. Check that the lender paid each installment on the correct parcel, and do not pay a second time. The county also runs an online lookup where you can pull a parcel's current and prior-year tax information, with years available back to 2003.

Frequently asked questions

What is the mailing address for Rock Island County tax?

Rock Island County Collector, PO Box 3277, Rock Island, IL 61204-3277, with the stub enclosed. A postmark on or before the due date is required, and other payment methods are safer given Postal Service delays.

Does Rock Island County take partial tax payments?

No. Partial installments are refused and installments are taken in order, with penalty interest included. Delinquent taxes likewise must be settled in one payment at the County Clerk.

When is the Rock Island County senior freeze deadline?

July 1. The application goes to the Chief County Assessment Office and has to be repeated annually. The income cap climbs from $65,000 for tax year 2025 to $79,000 for 2028.

How long can sold Rock Island County taxes be redeemed?

Two and a half to three years after the sale, as chosen by the tax buyer. Pay the County Clerk's Delinquent Tax Division, reachable at 309-558-3562, in cash, by cashier's check, by certified check or by money order.

What is the Rock Island County assessment office phone number?

Call the Chief County Assessment Office at 309-558-3660. It keeps weekday hours, 8 to 4:30, on the second floor of the County Office Building at 1504 Third Avenue in Rock Island.

Cash Home Buyers in Illinois
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

Selling in Saline County? Get a Cash Offer

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Saline County?

Who to call about a Saline County bill

Four offices in the Harrisburg courthouse, all at 10 East Poplar Street, share the job: the treasurer, the assessor, the Board of Review and the clerk and recorder. Weekday hours at each run from eight to four.

  • Treasurer, (618) 252-6915: mails bills, takes payments and runs the yearly tax sale.
  • Assessor, Suite 23, (618) 252-0691: holds a record card on every parcel and gives out exemption forms. Owners get their own card at no charge, and anyone else pays $0.75 a page.
  • Board of Review: three people named by the county board. They sign off on homestead exemptions and have the last word on assessment complaints.
  • Clerk and Recorder, Suite 17, (618) 253-8197: redemption of sold taxes and recording of deeds.

Township assessors work beneath the county, grouped as Harrisburg; East Eldorado, Cottage and Rector; Galatia, Long Branch and Tate; Brushy and Raleigh; Carrier Mills; and Independence, Mountain and Stonefort. For a record card or a value question, start with the county office.

When bills go out and what late costs

One bill goes out each year, split into two installments that usually fall in October and November. Read the dates printed on your own bill.

A payment that does not reach the treasurer, or carry a postmark, by its due date gains 1.5% for every month it stays late. Once the second installment passes, the tax counts as delinquent and heads toward publication and sale. The treasurer first has to mail a final notice by certified mail to the owner of record in the county system, so an owner who moved away should keep a current mailing address on file.

The sale itself happens once a year, generally in January. Bidders compete on interest, starting at 9% and falling as far as 0%, and the winner pays the treasurer the tax plus the cost of the sale.

After a tax sale: redemption

Only the debt is sold. The owner keeps the right to buy it back through the County Clerk, and the shortest redemption period is two years from the sale. A home with one to six units gets at least two and a half years, and the buyer may stretch any deadline to a limit of three.

Delinquent tax steps in Saline County
StepWhat happens
Second installment missedTaxes become delinquent and go to publication and sale
Annual tax saleHeld in January, bidding from 9% down to 0%
Notice to ownerThe buyer mails a Take Notice within 4.5 months of the sale
Redemption period2.5 years minimum for residential properties of one to six units, 2 years for other property, extendable to 3 years
Court filingBuyer petitions three to six months before the period ends
Tax deedCourt orders the clerk to issue the deed if all requirements are met

Buying the tax back takes one full payment in certified funds. The clerk accepts cash, a cashier's check, a certified check or a money order made out to the Saline County Clerk, with the parcel number written on it. An estimate of redemption is available on request. When a later year also goes unpaid, the buyer can purchase that year as well and add it to the total with a 12% annual penalty.

Homestead and other exemptions

The assessor's office lists a general homestead exemption and a set of programs for seniors, service members and disabled owners. Check that the general exemption shows on the bill for any house you live in.

  • General Homestead: takes up to $6,000 off the assessed value of an owner-occupied home.
  • Senior Citizen Homestead: $5,000 off for an owner who turns 65 by December 31 of the tax year. The senior has to apply in person, and the county mails a renewal each January.
  • Senior Assessment Freeze: 65 or older with household income under $65,000, a limit that rises to $75,000 beginning in 2026. File by July 1 and renew yearly.
  • Homestead Improvement: a new deck, garage, porch or room is exempt for four years, up to $25,000 of assessed value.
  • Disabled Persons: $2,000 off, filed by July 1 each year.
  • Returning service members: $5,000 off for two years, the year of return and the one after.

Disabled veteran exemptions range from $2,500 off up to full exemption on the first $250,000 of assessed value, depending on the rating the VA certifies.

How to challenge a valuation

Call the assessor with your parcel number. If the answer does not settle it, take a complaint to the Board of Review, which examines assessments, corrects individual ones and decides complaints.

The window for a formal complaint is short, usually about 30 days after assessments are published, so ask the Saline assessor for your township's publication date the moment a change notice arrives. Bring the property record card, the price you paid if you bought recently, and sales of comparable houses nearby.

Farm and timber parcels follow separate valuation rules, and the assessor's office posts a wooded acreage publication and a farmland valuation page for those owners.

Where deeds are recorded

The county clerk and recorder takes the deed. The same office lists the Illinois Real Estate Transfer Declaration, called MyDEC, among its forms, and that declaration is filed through the state Department of Revenue.

Phone (618) 253-8197 before a closing to ask what recording costs today. If the property carries a sold tax, redemption runs through that same office, so keep the parcel number handy.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Saline County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Saline County housing context

Saline County is a rural stretch of southern Illinois with Harrisburg as both seat and largest city. Eldorado is the other city, and U.S. Route 45 ties Eldorado, Harrisburg and Carrier Mills together. Population is shrinking: 22,772 people in the July 2025 estimate against 23,768 in the 2020 count.

Roughly 72.5% of occupied homes are lived in by their owners, the middle home value is $94,300, and median gross rent is $726. The county had 11,558 housing units in 2025 and no building permits that year. With values this low, a few hundred dollars of back tax or penalty is a bigger share of the price than in a pricier market, so clearing it before listing helps.

Selling a house with unpaid tax

A Saline County house with unpaid tax is still sellable. Begin by learning whether the tax is merely unpaid or already sold: the treasurer answers for the current year and the clerk for earlier ones.

  • Unpaid and not yet sold: the treasurer can state the amount plus the 1.5% monthly penalty.
  • Sold in January: the clerk's estimate of redemption adds interest and fees.
  • Court petition filed: the final Take Notice names the last day to redeem and the hearing date, so reach the clerk before that day.

Hand those numbers to the title company so the payoff is fixed before closing. A rough house with a long redemption clock may still draw an offer from a cash buyer.

Frequently asked questions

Who collects property tax in Saline County, Illinois?

The Saline County Treasurer, at 10 East Poplar Street in Harrisburg, phone (618) 252-6915. One bill a year goes out with two installments. After a sale, the County Clerk handles redemption.

What does a late Saline County tax payment cost?

The penalty is 1.5% per month on any payment not received or postmarked by its due date. Tax still unpaid after the second installment is delinquent and can be sold.

How long can I buy back sold taxes in Saline County?

At least 2.5 years from the sale for a home of one to six units, and at least two years for other property. The tax buyer can stretch the deadline to three years. Call the County Clerk for an estimate of redemption.

Where do I apply for a homestead exemption in Saline County?

At the assessor's office, Suite 23 at 10 East Poplar Street in Harrisburg, where applications for every exemption are kept. A senior exemption must be requested in person. The Board of Review approves or denies homestead exemptions.

Which Saline County office files my deed?

The County Clerk and Recorder, Suite 17 of the courthouse at 10 East Poplar Street. Its forms list includes the Illinois Real Estate Transfer Declaration, MyDEC. Call (618) 253-8197 first to ask about fees.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Sangamon County?

Sangamon County offices and who does what

The treasurer collects, the Supervisor of Assessments and the Board of Review deal with values and complaints, and the county clerk steps in after a tax is sold. Most of them work out of the County Building at 200 South Ninth Street in Springfield, where the county seat doubles as the state capital.

  • Treasurer, first floor, Room 109, weekday hours of 8:30 to 5:00: payments and bill questions. Programs and deferral questions go to (217) 753-6800.
  • Supervisor of Assessments, (217) 753-6805: parcel numbers, exemption forms and complaint forms.
  • County Clerk, (217) 753-6701: estimates of redemption on sold taxes.
  • Recorder, first floor, (217) 535-3150: deeds.

The county's property tax website finds a parcel by number, address or owner name, shows its billing details, and prints exemption and complaint forms. The county is divided into 26 active townships, among them Capital Township, which matches the City of Springfield.

Payment calendar and how to pay

Installments fall once in early summer and once in early fall. For tax year 2025, payable in 2026, they were due June 5 and September 4. The unpaid balance goes to the annual sale in early November, and the treasurer posts tentative dates each spring.

  • E-check, card, phone and drive-thru payments stop at 5 p.m. two days before the sale. Walk-in payments at the Treasurer's office close at 5 p.m. the day before, with cash or check only on that final day.
  • E-check on the county site has no fee. Card payments add a convenience fee set by the card companies.
  • Card payments by phone go through (888) 834-3729. Checks go to the Sangamon County Collector, PO Box 19400, Springfield, IL 62794-9400, and must carry a postmark on or before the due date.

Late penalties begin after each due date.

Assessment complaint deadlines

The deadline depends on the township. The county publishes assessment changes one township at a time and gives each its own filing deadline, roughly a month after publication. In 2026 those deadlines run from early September to late December, and Capital and Gardner townships have already closed.

To print a complaint, find your parcel on the county's property tax website and choose Assessment Complaint under the taxpayer forms. For Rochester, Curran and Fancy Creek townships, call the Supervisor of Assessments for dates.

Homestead and other exemptions

The Supervisor of Assessments describes a general exemption, a senior exemption, a senior freeze, an improvement exemption and a handful for service members and disabled owners.

  • General Homestead: as much as $6,000 off equalized assessed value for a home you occupy. Apply by January 31 of the tax year. It needs no yearly renewal, and it stays behind when you move, so a new home needs a fresh application.
  • Senior Citizen: $5,000 off for owners 65 or older, also filed by January 31.
  • Senior Assessment Freeze: household income of $75,000 or less and a year of ownership and occupancy before you apply. Forms circulate from April 1 to July 1, and July 1 is the yearly deadline.
  • Homestead Improvement: additions, garages, decks or porches that add up to $75,000 of market value stay off the tax for as long as four years.
  • Disabled Persons: $2,000 off, renewed annually. Returning service members: $5,000 off.

The treasurer also describes a senior deferral that puts a lien on the home, with the deferred tax due when the home sells or the owner dies. Anyone selling with a deferral in place should request a payoff figure from the treasurer.

If a bill goes unpaid

The tax is sold at the annual sale, and from then on you settle it with the County Clerk instead of the Treasurer. Call the clerk at (217) 753-6701 for an estimate of redemption, which adds late fees, interest and sale fees to the original amount.

Sold taxes take certified funds, a cashier's check, a money order or cash payable to the Sangamon County Clerk. Neither personal checks nor credit cards are taken for them. You may also contact the tax buyer and ask whether payments in installments are acceptable, though a refusal sends you back to the clerk.

Current-year bills are easier: a personal check or cash made out to the County Treasurer and Collector works. A duplicate bill comes from the treasurer, and buyers who want to bid at the sale register with the treasurer first.

Sangamon County housing context

Sangamon sits near the middle of Illinois. The county had an estimated 194,170 residents in July 2025, down from 196,343 in 2020. The middle value for an owner-occupied home is $176,300, median gross rent is $983 and median household income is $75,357. Owners occupy 71.3% of homes, and the county counted 93,820 housing units and 224 building permits in 2025. Springfield District 186, Ball-Chatham, Rochester, Pleasant Plains and Williamsville are among the school districts with territory here.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Sangamon County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Deeds and transfer tax

A sale or gift needs a fresh deed, prepared, signed, notarized and recorded with the Sangamon County Recorder. If a sale is for $100 or more, the PTAX-203 transfer declaration travels with it.

It costs $64 to record a deed on standard 8.5 by 11 paper and $84 for a non-standard document. Transfer tax stamps are priced at $0.50 per $500 of value for the state, plus $0.25 per $500 for the county. A gift escapes the tax when the deed carries the exemption paragraph. Mailed originals are returned in three to five business days, by the office's goal, and title companies can use eRecording.

Listing a house that owes taxes

You can list a Sangamon County house with taxes owed, but you need two figures first: what the treasurer shows as due now, and the clerk's estimate of redemption for any sold year.

  • Open the parcel on the county's property tax website for billing details.
  • Ask the clerk whether an earlier year was sold, and what clearing it costs.
  • Find out whether a freeze or deferral applies, since a deferral is repaid at sale.

Give the figures to the title company so the payoff is settled at the closing table. A house needing repairs and carrying back taxes may find a cash buyer who takes it in present condition, and a cash sale skips the lender's appraisal.

Frequently asked questions

How do I pay Sangamon County property taxes?

Use e-check on the county website, which has no fee, call (888) 834-3729 to pay by card, mail a check to PO Box 19400, Springfield, IL 62794-9400, or pay in Room 109 of the County Building. Card payments add a convenience fee.

When are Sangamon County installments due?

Once in early summer and once in early fall. For tax year 2025 they were June 5 and September 4. Check the treasurer's page each spring for the next dates.

How do I get a redemption estimate in Sangamon County?

Call the County Clerk at (217) 753-6701 and ask for an estimate of redemption. Pay with certified funds, a cashier's check, a money order or cash made out to the Sangamon County Clerk, never with a credit card or personal check.

Does a homestead exemption follow me to a new house?

No. The general exemption does not transfer, so the next owner who lives in the home files a new application. The deadline is January 31 for the tax year, and the exemption takes up to $6,000 off assessed value.

Which Sangamon County office files my deed?

The Sangamon County Recorder, on the first floor of the County Building at 200 South Ninth Street in Springfield, phone (217) 535-3150. A sale of $100 or more needs a PTAX-203. Mailed originals go with a check for the exact fee.

Cash Home Buyers in Illinois

Selling in Scott County? Get a Cash Offer

We buy Scott County houses as-is and reply with a written cash offer.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Scott County?
We buy Scott County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Scott County property tax at a glance

Scott County is small, and property tax questions land on a handful of courthouse desks in Winchester, the county seat, at 35 East Market Street. The 2020 census counted 4,949 people, and the July 1, 2025 estimate is 4,866, down 4.1%. The county has 2,377 housing units, and owners hold 79.0% of occupied homes.

The typical owner-reported home value is $96,400, and the middle renter pays $689 a month gross. With values at that level, a small change in condition or tax status can swing how fast a house sells, so it pays to know your bill and your paperwork before you list.

Which offices handle assessments, bills and records?

Three offices cover most property tax questions: the Assessor, the Treasurer and the County Clerk. Each has its own page at scottcoil.gov, and each does a separate job in the yearly cycle.

  • The Assessor (Supervisor of Assessments) applies exemptions, maintains the parcel numbers and map files, sends assessment notices, runs the appeal process and certifies the roll to the County Clerk. Call 217-742-5751 or write to assessor@scottcoil.gov.
  • The Treasurer collects real estate and mobile home taxes, keeps the revenue records, pays out the money to taxing bodies and answers parcel questions.
  • The County Clerk works with the Treasurer on the yearly delinquent tax sale. The county site also has property record and fee schedule pages for deed and record requests.

The assessor's fee list was updated on April 27, 2026. A property record card costs $1.00, copies are $0.50 per page, a letter-size printed aerial map is $10.00 and an emailed PDF aerial map is $5.00. Pull the record card before you list. It shows the house characteristics the assessment rests on, and a wrong square footage or bedroom count is easy to fix at this stage.

Due dates and how bills work

The Treasurer posts payment dates at the top of its page each year. Bills go out in early summer and are payable in two installments, one in July and one in September. In 2026 the bills were mailed June 8, with installments due July 17 and September 18. Call the Treasurer for the schedule on your next bill.

Illinois bills a year behind, so taxes for one year are billed and collected the next. A house sold in autumn still has a bill coming that covers the year the seller owned it, and the closing statement has to deal with that. Mobile home taxes go through the same office on their own bills.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Scott County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Exemptions that lower a Scott County bill

Each exemption reduces the equalized assessed value that the rate is applied to. Apply through the Chief County Assessment Office, which takes both first applications and renewals. Ask whether the previous owner's exemption carries over or needs a new filing in your name.

Exemptions on the Scott County exemptions page
ExemptionBenefitForm or proof
General homesteadRise in assessed value over the 1977 figure, up to $6,000Owner-occupied residence
Senior citizens assessment freezeHolds the assessed value; income ceiling rises starting with the 2026 yearFederal return with every schedule
Returning service members$5,000 off for two straight tax yearsForm PTAX-341
Persons with disabilities$2,000 off each yearYearly Form PTAX-343-R
Disabled service members, standard$2,500 at a 30% to 50% rating, $5,000 at 50% to 70%, full exemption at 70% or moreTotal value under $250,000
Specially adapted housingAs much as $100,000 off assessed valueService-connected disability
Homestead improvementNew rooms, remodels and rebuilds shielded for four years, up to $75,000 fair cash value ($25,000 assessed)Permit and completed work

The senior freeze ceiling comes from Public Act 104-0452, signed December 12, 2025. Once 2028 is past, the ceiling holds at $79,000 unless lawmakers act again.

How to appeal your assessment

The window is short. Section 16-55(d) of the Property Tax Code gives an owner 30 calendar days from publication of the assessment list to get a written complaint to the Board of Review. A mailed complaint counts from its postmark, and a courier package from the shipper's label, so keep the receipt.

The board is told to weigh compulsory sales, including ones the owner submits, when they share the property's features and condition. Start with the Assessor's record card and find out what drove the new value. Then collect recent sales of similar Scott County houses. An owner who loses can carry the dispute to the Property Tax Appeal Board. Only the assessed value is in play, because the taxing districts set the rates.

What happens when taxes go unpaid?

Each year the Treasurer, with help from the County Clerk, sells off delinquent real estate taxes, delinquent mobile home taxes and unpaid special assessments. A parcel left unpaid can end up in that sale.

Call the Treasurer's Office for the balance on the parcel, the sale date and any earlier year left open. The County Clerk explains redemption steps and costs, so ask for the balance in writing. Settle any open year before you list, since the buyer's title search will turn up the same thing.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Scott County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with taxes owed

An unpaid bill does not block a sale, but the buyer will expect it cleared by closing. The closing agent usually gets the balance from the Treasurer, pays it out of the seller's share and then records the deed.

  • Section 31-10 sets the state transfer tax at 50 cents per $500 block of stated value. A transfer declaration (PTAX-203, or MyDec online) goes in with the deed.
  • Phone the County Clerk before closing day about recording fees and any county stamp.
  • Of the county's 2,388 housing units in the 2020 count, 12.0% were vacant, so buyers have plenty of choices and tend to push on price when a file looks messy.

Owners who inherited a house, cannot fund repairs or have fallen behind on taxes have three paths: a listing, a private deal or a sale to a buyer who takes the house in its present state. The third path skips repair work, though the tax payoff is still settled at closing.

Before you list: a short checklist

A few errands in Winchester make a Scott County sale smoother. Start with the Assessor's record card for your parcel and check the square footage and room count. Next, ask the Treasurer for a written balance and confirm that no earlier year is open. Then ask the Assessor which exemptions are on the parcel today, because a buyer's lender will see them on the bill.

Bring your parcel number and a photo ID, and expect to pay the small fees above for copies. If an addition or remodel went in during your ownership, find the permit paperwork, since the improvement exemption and the record card both depend on it.

Frequently asked questions

Where is the Scott County courthouse?

The county seat is Winchester, at 35 East Market Street. The Treasurer, Assessor and County Clerk each have their own page at scottcoil.gov.

When are Scott County property taxes due?

Bills go out in early summer, with two installments in July and September. In 2026 they were due July 17 and September 18. The Treasurer's Office can give the next set of dates.

How much is the general homestead exemption?

The maximum is $6,000, measured against the 1977 equalized assessed value, for counties outside the Cook County area.

How long do I have to file an assessment complaint?

Thirty calendar days from publication of the assessment list. Put the complaint in writing, send it to the Board of Review and keep the postmark or tracking label.

Can I sell a Scott County house with unpaid property tax?

Yes. The closing agent gets the balance from the Treasurer and pays it from the seller's share, so the buyer does not inherit the debt.

Who does what on a St. Clair County tax bill

Five county offices share the job. The Assessor estimates each parcel's value, the Board of Review decides disputes, the County Clerk works out the rate, the Treasurer mails and collects the bill, and the Clerk also runs the annual tax sale. A homeowner who needs help often has to call two of them.

The Assessor's page lists direct lines for common errands, all through the county switchboard at 618-277-6600:

  • Tax rate questions: County Clerk, extension 2365.
  • Change of address for tax bills and assessment notices: Mapping and Platting, extension 2533.
  • Mobile home tax: Treasurer, extension 2451. Delinquent mobile home tax: County Clerk, extension 2363.

Before listing, gather three items: the Treasurer's payment record for your parcel, the Assessor's property record card and a clear idea of how the year's tax will be divided at closing.

Housing numbers for the county

St. Clair County sits directly east of St. Louis in the Metro East area, with Belleville as the county seat and largest city. Population is estimated at 250,708 for July 1, 2025, down from 257,400 at the 2020 count. Midpoint value for an owned home is $180,300, rent for a typical unit is $1,090, and 68.4% of homes have an owner living in them. Half of households earn more than $73,854.

Owning costs $1,645 a month at the midpoint for mortgage holders and $645 for owners with no loan. The county has 100,846 households averaging 2.47 people. Treat these as county-wide markers and look at actual sales near your own address, since East St. Louis, O'Fallon, Fairview Heights and Belleville price very differently.

Commuters value the interstates (I-55, I-64, I-70 and I-255), the 11 MetroLink stations and the short drive to Scott Air Force Base, so mention proximity to those in a listing if it applies.

Property tax due dates

Each year's tax is billed in the following year and paid in two installments. The Treasurer posts a schedule for each bill, and the dates are marked tentative until the bills go out. The pattern stays much the same from year to year, so use it as a guide and call the Treasurer for the exact dates on your next bill.

Typical St. Clair County collection calendar
StepWhen it usually falls
First installment dueStart of July
Second installment dueStart of September
Final payment before the saleEnd of October
Annual tax saleEarly November

The Treasurer also sets a mid-September deadline to avoid newspaper publication. Electronic payment stops at 3 p.m. on that day and on the final payment day, and a postmark earns no grace.

What a late or unpaid bill costs

A late installment picks up a state-set penalty of 1.5% of what remains unpaid, and another 1.5% is added every thirty days. The coupon on your bill prints the amount owed with penalty. Only the Treasurer's office accepts partial payments, since collector banks refuse them.

The county can sell the lien on a parcel with unpaid tax. A homeowner whose property is the principal dwelling, with no more than six apartments, can redeem for two and one-half years, while owners of other property get two years. To redeem, the owner pays the tax plus penalties and interest, and skipping redemption can end in loss of the property. If you are selling, clear any balance at closing.

  • An escrow account does not shift responsibility. The owner answers for the bill whatever the bank or servicer arranged.
  • The Treasurer does not report to credit bureaus, so a late bill does not touch your score.
  • Pay by mail, in person, at listed collector banks through the second due date, or online. Cards cost 2.5% with a $2.00 minimum.

How to contest your assessment

Start by reading your bill and the Assessor's property record card, looking for missing exemptions and wrong facts about the house. The Assessor measures a home's outside perimeter for square footage, so your interior measurement will be smaller. Assessed value equals one-third of estimated market value, and the estimate rests on recent sales of similar homes.

If talking to the Assessor does not settle it, take the case to the elected three-member Board of Review at 10 Public Square, Belleville, IL 62220. The 30-day filing period starts once the Assessor revises assessments. Useful evidence includes a photo of your house, photos and property record cards for three comparable homes, or a recent appraisal, sales contract, settlement statement or deed. The Board's office must have your papers five days or more ahead of the hearing, or the assessment is upheld as is. A further appeal goes to the Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board.

A separate route, the Tax Objection Complaint, goes through the Circuit Clerk. It mostly serves rate disputes and is due within 75 days after the second installment date.

Exemptions and deferrals

Homeowners can claim the general homestead exemption for an owner-occupied residence, and returning servicemembers and people with disabilities have separate ones. The county posts three senior programs on its Treasurer page.

  • Senior homestead exemption: takes $5,000 off the assessed value of a home owned and lived in by someone 65 or older.
  • Senior assessment freeze: locks the assessed value for qualifying owners. The Assessor, at 618-825-2704, sends the application.
  • Senior tax deferral: the state pays the tax and records a lien, then recovers it with 6% annual interest when the home is sold or transferred. Plan for repayment at closing if the owner used it. The Treasurer, at 618-825-2440, supplies the forms.

The Treasurer also runs a monthly payment plan for current-tax homeowners who hold the homeowner occupied exemption. Sign-up begins in August and payments start in September, with no change to the due dates.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy St. Clair County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How the tax is split when a house sells

Tax arrives a year behind the period it covers, so the closing statement hands the buyer a credit for the months the seller held the house. Look in your closing papers for that proportionate share.

Pull the Treasurer's record for the parcel first, and find out whether the newest bill is paid, open or already sold. Estate houses, rentals and empty properties are the likeliest to have a delinquency. For a tax sale question, phone the County Clerk at 618-277-6600. For an exemption question, phone the Board of Review at 618-825-2489.

Put the parcel number, the latest bill and your exemption paperwork in one folder. Any buyer, cash or financed, will ask for them. If a senior deferral is on the parcel, ask the Treasurer for the payoff before you sign a contract so the lien is cleared at the table and nothing lingers after the deed is recorded.

A cash buyer will usually close on whatever date the title company can clear, and the tax balance is paid out of your proceeds. That makes the first phone call to the Treasurer the most useful step you can take before you list.

Frequently asked questions

How many installments does St. Clair County collect?

Two a year, typically around the start of July and the start of September. The Treasurer marks the dates tentative until bills go out and can confirm the dates for your next bill.

How fast does a late St. Clair County bill grow?

At 1.5% of the balance every month, a rate set by the state. The coupon on your bill shows the total with penalty.

When must I file a St. Clair County assessment appeal?

Inside 30 days of the Assessor's revised assessments, with the Board of Review. A rate challenge through the Circuit Clerk runs on a separate 75-day clock from the second installment date.

Can a St. Clair County owner get the house back after a tax sale?

Yes, by redeeming. A principal dwelling with six or fewer apartments gets two and one-half years and other property two years, at the price of the tax plus penalties and interest.

Which St. Clair County office should a senior call for tax relief?

Start with the Treasurer, 618-825-2440, for deferral forms and the Assessor, 618-825-2704, for the freeze. If the $5,000 senior homestead exemption is missing from your bill, call the Board of Review, 618-825-2489.

Who to call about a Stephenson County tax bill

Stephenson County splits the work between three desks in Freeport. The Treasurer and Collector sends and takes payment on bills, at the Stewart Centre, 50 West Douglas Street, Suite 503 (fifth floor), 815-235-8264, with a counter that opens at 8:30 in the morning and closes at 4:30 on weekdays. That office does not set assessed values, exemptions or bill amounts.

  • Assessment questions, exemptions, mapping, address clarifications and assessment complaints: the Assessor's office, 815-235-8260.
  • Redemption amounts after a tax sale: the County Clerk, 815-235-8289.
  • Filing a complaint: the clerk of the Board of Review, 50 West Douglas Street, Suite 502.

One local wrinkle matters for owners inside the city. Freeport Township assesses its own parcels, and their numbers begin with 18. The county assessor handles the other 17 townships. The Freeport Township Assessor is at 524 W. Stephenson St., Suite 214, 815-232-6131.

Housing in Stephenson County

Freeport anchors Stephenson County, in northwestern Illinois. The county has an estimated 43,220 residents, down from 44,630 at the 2020 count. Of its 21,369 housing units, 10.2 percent were vacant, and among occupied homes 70.4 percent were owner-occupied. Roughly 54 percent of residents live in urban areas and 46 percent in rural ones.

Cold winters put furnace age and roof condition high on a buyer's list, so keep service records and roof receipts handy. A house inside Freeport and one on a rural parcel can differ in which assessor covers them, so check the parcel number before you compare tax bills.

Payment dates and deadlines

One bill goes out in May for both halves, and both can be paid together by the first date. The calendar below repeats each year with small shifts, so ask the Treasurer for the exact dates on your bill.

Usual Stephenson County payment calendar
StepWhen it usually falls
Online lookup and payment opensLate May
First installment dueLate June
Second installment dueEarly September
Last day to pay before the tax saleEarly November

A mailed installment is on time when the post office postmarks it by midnight of the due date. A postage meter stamp does not count, so leave margin. The last day before the tax sale works differently: payments must be received, not just postmarked, by the end of that business day. Partial payments are returned, because Illinois law does not allow the collector to accept them.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Stephenson County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Where can I pay my Stephenson County tax bill?

Five routes are open. Every route needs the barcoded coupon, original or reprint, and banks ask for it too.

  • By mail to Stephenson County Collector, 50 W. Douglas St., Suite 503, Freeport, IL 61032.
  • In the payment dropbox just inside the Stewart Centre lobby. Cash does not go in the box.
  • In person at the treasurer's office on the fifth floor.
  • At most banks in the county. Fifth Third Bank and credit unions cannot take them.
  • Online through the county portal or your bank's bill pay. E-check carries a flat $2.95 fee that covers up to 99 payments, and none of the fees go to the county.

A lost bill can be printed free from the portal. An exact duplicate costs $1.00 per parcel for an owner and $5.00 for anyone else, and a veteran pays no duplicate fee. A bill that never arrives still carries the tax and the penalty. If your mailing address is wrong, call the Assessor's office at 815-235-8260, which needs a signature on file to change it.

How a Stephenson County bill is calculated

A bill is a taxable value times a rate. Assessors value each parcel as of January 1 and target one-third of fair market value, and a past assessment publication reported a median level of 33.33 percent. Credits and exemptions come off the assessed figure.

The rate depends on where the parcel sits. The county has 104 tax districts, and each parcel lies in its own mix of school, township, road, fire, park, library and county bodies. The county clerk's extension division divides each body's levy by its tax base. Exemptions you may qualify for include:

  • Owner Occupied Exemption.
  • Senior Citizen Homestead Exemption and Senior Citizen Freeze.
  • Homestead Improvement Exemption.
  • Disabled Veteran Exemption.

More than 26,000 bills go out each year. Property is taxed, not people, and each bill rests on the prior year's assessment for a full calendar year.

How to dispute your assessment

Talk to the township assessor or the chief county assessment office first. If that does not settle it, a written complaint must reach the Board of Review no later than 30 calendar days after your township's change list is published (35 ILCS 200/16-55). Once that date passes, the board cannot take complaints for the township.

Forms and instructions come from the assessment office at 815-235-8260, in person or online, and the completed form goes to the clerk of the Board of Review. A complaint mailed through the post office counts as filed on its postmark date. The board is barred by law from accepting late ones.

A taxpayer who disagrees with the board has 30 days from written notice of its decision to petition the state Property Tax Appeal Board, or may sue in circuit court (35 ILCS 200/16-160). Only value is on the table. Rates and bill totals are set by other bodies.
